item.title: Arizona Cardinals Daily Links: Trey McBride leads NFL in receptions, 2nd in yards after Week One
item.description: Trey McBride leads the league in receptions (9) after Week 1 while also being second in receiving yards (95).
item.content:encoded:
So no one’s surprise, star tight end Trey McBride sits at the top of the NFL in at least on category after the Cardinals’ Week One win over the Chargers.

With nine receptions on Sunday, he sits atop the league after just one game. That’s one reception ahead of Isaiah Likely of the New York Giants. As for his 95 receiving yards, that’s actually a distant second to the Bills’ Dalton Kincaid who had 130 yards on just five reception in their win over the Texans.

McBride will face the reigning Super Bowl champs in Week Two and will have his hands full with a talented secondary. Will he be able to keep up his hot start to the season?

item.title: NFL news, live updates: Jaxson Dart dazzles vs. Cowboys, Kyler Murray suffers concussion in Vikings debut
item.description: Follow along with the latest NFL news coming out of Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
The first NFL Sunday of the season is officially in the books, with Week 1 jam-packed with action.

The Sunday action capped with the new-look New York Giants putting a hurting on their division-rival Dallas Cowboys. Giants quarterback Jackson Dart delivered three touchdown passes and rushed for 54 yards in the 28-20 victory.

The early window was action-packed (and absolutely filled to the brim with points), headlined by a Buffalo Bills-Houston Texans thriller for the ages where Josh Allen led a tremendous comeback effort in the final 90 seconds with a 96-yard drive ending in a touchdown to win 36-31.

The Chicago Bears also stunned with a 59-point effort against the Carolina Panthers after head coach Ben Johnson expressed hope to finish the year with the "highest-scoring offense ever" in the offseason. Third-year quarterback Caleb Williams was 21-of-29 passing for 269 yards and two touchdowns, adding another 65 yards and two touchdowns on the ground on the way to the win.

On the injury front, there was (unfortunately) plenty of news coming out of Sunday, starting with the Rams announcing star DE Myles Garrett will undergo a knee procedure that will force him to miss time and be placed on injured reserve. He's set to miss at least the next four games of the season. New Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray also took a scary hit in his debut for the team, exiting Sunday's win with a concussion, replaced in the lineup by backup Carson Wentz.

item.title: Ashton jeanty making history
item.description: Young running back is making history scoring as a receiver
item.content:encoded:
We all could see this coming.

Last year, as a rookie, Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty showed prowess as a receiver out of the backfield as he had 55 catches and five touchdown catches. This offseason, new head coach Klint Kubiak stated that the goal was to get the No. 6 overall pick in last year’s draft very involved in the receiving game.

And it showed in the very first game. Jeanty had two receiving touchdown in a win over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday.

It was his second game of his young career in which he had games game multiple receiving touchdowns. He is just the second play since the 1970 merger to accomplish the feat in his first 20 games of his career according to the Raiders’ PR department.

We can see Jeanty add many more receiving milestones this season.

item.title: Matt LaFleur has a lot of problems to navigate
item.description: Not a great situation for Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
Bad losses tend to put everything in the larger universe of Packers-related takes in free fall for a while, but at a certain point, it feels like even the most outlandish takes aren’t exaggerating anymore.

Dating back to last year’s Broncos game, the Packers have collapsed again and again, week after week, and every time it happens, it feels like we reach a new critical mass of takes. I’ve heard from readers and listeners since Sunday suggesting all manner of causes for the Packers’ trouble, ranging from the implausible (the league told the refs to penalize the Packers as retribution for the hit on Kyler Murray) to the absurd (the Packers lost because Jordan Love has bad body language). But the weirder and more gut-wrenching ways in which the Packers lose, the harder it becomes to dismiss anything.

Are the Packers just cosmically unlucky? I mean, even if you think Matt LaFleur is the worst coach in the world, you’d think things would break his way a couple of times in the span of what’s now a six-game losing streak. How many random drops or weird bounces or phantom flags can possibly go against one team in one stretch?

All that to say, as exhausting as the wild and wacky and weird takes might be right now, it’s almost impossible to find your way out of the fever swamps, too. Much like the Packers, we’re going to have to ride this out to the bitter end.

item.title: NFL power rankings, Week 2: NY Giants take massive jump
item.description: NFL analysts noticed what the Giants did to the Cowboys.
item.content:encoded:
Sunday night’s impressive victory over the Dallas Cowboys has resulted in the New York Giants taking a massive leap in Week 2 NFL power rankings. The Giants have moved from No. 23 in our aggregated rankings from around the Internet to No. 16, the league’s midpoint.

ESPN | No. 18

Week 1 result: Beat the Cowboys 28-20
Non-QB newcomer debut: TE Isaiah Likely

Likely was quarterback Jaxson Dart’s go-to receiver, catching two third-down passes on the game-ending drive to go along with two touchdowns earlier. Overall, Likely caught all eight targets for 78 yards. The chemistry with Dart throughout training camp carried over to the season, to the point where it’s easy to see Likely having a huge campaign despite never reaching 500 receiving yards in any of his four years with the Ravens. The performance was no surprise to coach John Harbaugh. “I mean, we paid him a lot,” Harbaugh said with a laugh. “That’s what we paid him for, and he did it.”

FOX Sports | No. 17

It’s a well-deserved leap in the rankings after John Harbaugh’s debut showed he has a tough, well-rounded and healthy team. When WR Malik Nabers is off his pitch count, this versatile offense is going to cause problems for everyone.

Pro Football Network | No. 23

The John Harbaugh era of New York Giants football kicked off in triumphant fashion. They defeated the Cowboys at home, coming away from Sunday night with a key divisional victory. Emotions were high with the Giants’ pregame ceremony honoring those affected by Sept. 11, and New York went home happy.

Jaxson Dart got it done through the air and on the ground, throwing for 230 and three passing touchdowns while rushing for 57 yards. The likes of Isaiah Likely and Cam Skattebo were key in the Giants’ victory, and the team’s run defense limited Dallas’ offense to just 3.8 yards per carry.

USA Today | No. 14

Don’t want to overrate them this early, but Sunday night’s victory over the Cowboys was no fluke. This was efficient, smashmouth, Harbaugh football, and the rest of the NFC East is officially on notice.

Yahoo Sports | No. 14

No team had a better offensive EPA per play through Sunday’s Week 1 games than the Giants. Not even the Bears, who scored 59 points. What stood out was the impact new tight end Isaiah Likely had. He led the Giants with eight catches for 78 yards and two touchdowns. If the Giants’ offense stays mostly healthy, perhaps this can be a surprise playoff team.

The Athletic | No. 18

What we learned: They might be for real

High expectations around the hiring of John Harbaugh were tempered by what seemed to be just an OK roster. But the Harbaugh era started smashingly, Jaxson Dart looked legit and the defense more than held its own against a good (or so we thought) Dallas offense.

Bleacher Report | No. 21

So maybe hiring John Harbaugh was a pretty good idea.

Offensively Sunday night, New York was ruthlessly efficient. Jaxson Dart was poised and accurate. Cam Skattebo didn’t have huge numbers, but he got the tough yards when he needed to. Tight end Isaiah Likely was a revelation in his first game with the team.

New York was 9-of-11 on third down. That’s nuts.

The defense remains a work in progress, but it made just enough plays against one of the NFL’s best offenses a year ago to win the day—and a second straight contest with the Cowboys at Met Life Stadium.

It’s still too early to say the Giants are good—the Dallas defense has been awful dating back to 2025. But they were in Week 1, and we’ll find out soon enough how sustainable the improvement is.

item.title: Do the Chicago Bears need to aggressively add to their defense?
item.description: In Week 1, the Bears looked like a championship-level team on offense. The defense, though, still has too many holes. Should they make a move?
item.content:encoded:
Soak it in. The Bears’ offense is what everyone has been asking for since Rex Grossman laid a 2006-sized egg. A modern offense capable of scoring at any time and in any manner.

And yet, this roster does not look ready to compete for a championship. Why? The defense remains flawed. While there were still some standout performances, namely from rookies Dillon Thieneman and Malik Muhammad, the defensive line and defensive backfield have major holes.

Do the Bears need to make a trade and add to their defense?

I’m 95% there.

There are only a few remaining reasons to be optimistic that the Bears defense can still improve.

First, they are still missing some key players in Kyler Gordon and Coby Bryant. However, the severity of Bryant’s injury and lack of clarity around Gordon means that you can’t necessarily count on either of them. If (very big if) Gordon can return and make the impact he is capable of, that could help lock up the middle of the field and push someone like Muhammad outside where he might be more comfortable. If (another big if) Bryant can return 3/4 of the way through the season, he can bring some range and playmaking to the back end. Hard to rely on either of those realities, but neither are impossible.

Another reason for tepid optimism is the early returns on the young players. Both Thieneman and Muhammad had standout performances. Still, there were things that need cleaning up, particularly Muhammad’s coverage in the slot. He was beaten a few times on quick crossers — proof that he still needs time to get better at this new position. Add in preseason stars Jordan van den Berg and Jayden Loving, and there is still potential for some real growth along the defensive front.

My final plea for patience is simply that the Bears defense was put in a few bad situations, giving the Panthers short fields. The Panthers had drives start at the Bears 42, Panthers 40, Bears 21, and Panthers 42. This is unsustainable for any defense — and a sticking point I am sure Head Coach Ben Johnson will make during the upcoming week.

Still, the Bears surrendered 24 first downs, 478 total yards, 7.7 yards per play, and four touchdowns on four trips to the red zone. This defense has a lot of issues that need to be addressed.

So what needs the most attention? I think two things come to mind.

The Bears still need an EDGE to complement Montez Sweat. Dayo Odeyingbo looked slightly better yesterday, but made mistakes and still lacked necessary impact. Austin Booker was remarkably absent during the game yesterday. Any optimism that he could be the game wrecker on the DL was put into question after his performance. So at a minimum, the Bears need a DE2 opposite Sweat to help generate pressure from the opposite side. Ideally, the Bears can secure an EDGE that can be a primary pass rusher and shift Sweat to DE2. A Kayvon Thibodeaux could be a more affordable option.

Shifting focus to the defensive backfield, and what was previously viewed as a team strength looks like a defensive weakness after Week 1. Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson were both burned on several instances, leading to chunk plays by players like Jalen Coker, Darren Waller, and Tetairoa McMillan. While the DL needs to put pressure on QBs sooner, both Johnson and Stevenson appeared to have a difficult time keeping up in man coverage. Given the importance of Johnson in particular, this should be sounding alarms across the Bears organization. He hasn’t looked quite right since his groin and core injuries early in the 2025 season.

While the addition of Kyler Gordon or a quick return of Coby Bryant could help cover the issues on the outside CBs, I am walking away deeply concerned with the issues at starting CB. If the Bears are going to take a swing, I am more inclined to do so on an impact CB. A guy like Joey Porter Jr. could push Jaylon Johnson to CB2 and give him better matchups. I think this type of addition could go a long way in improving the pass defense for the Bears.

The Bears already have a ton of resources wrapped up in the defense, but given the initial returns on offense, Ryan Poles should pull out all of the stops to ensure that the defense can contribute to a legitimate championship run.

Now it’s your turn! Do the Bears need to aggressively add to their defense? Sound off in the comments!

item.title: Week 1 Film Review: Highlights from the All 22
item.description: The Film is Promising for the 0-1 Saints
item.content:encoded:
After experiencing the Saints vs. Lions, I could not wait until the game film was uploaded to be able to see the ins and outs of the team so that true evaluations on the performance could be made. As I went to bed Sunday night, I had no idea what was in store for me — 7 hours of nightmare in the form of Mike Pereira slowly moving his hand back and forth while patronizingly explaining the definition of a forward pass.

Takeaways from the Film

Vernon Broughton has Arrived

Though he plays a position that hardly shows up in the stat book and can go overlooked by the naked eye during the live broadcast, Vernon Broughton had a very good showing in his first regular-season action since Week 2 of last year. This was most noticeable when he lined up against Penei Sewell (one of the top linemen in the league), where Broughton was able to win multiple reps against the three-time first-team All-Pro. Although the sample size is small, if the Texas product can continue this trajectory, he will be viewed as a Trey Hendrickson-level steal by the Saints in the third round of last year’s draft.

Stutsman vs Werner

Both linebackers logged quality plays opposite Kaden Ellis this Sunday as they were faced with a tough challenge vs. the Lions. After watching the film, it was clear that each has their own strengths, but it seems like Stutsman is making the case to compete for the starting role throughout the year. Werner played like a savvy veteran and used his instincts to make multiple plays, including a nice TFL on Jahmyr Gibbs and an exceptional pass breakup down the middle of the field. Stutsman, on the other hand, was out of place on some plays but was able to recover due to his superior athletic ability. This is a great sign for the Saints, as the competition between the two seems to have them both playing good football against a very talented Lions offense.

2-Point Play

The refs’ worst mistake in the game was missing the pass interference call in the end zone on Bryce Lance for the game-winning 2-point conversion. When watching the play live, I knew people would wonder how Olave wasn’t targeted, and I’m happy to weigh in. The Saints ran a modified version of the “Spot” concept (shown above), which is a great play call in this area. The read is simple, and after the initial motion by Olave to the interior of the 3-receiver bunch, Tyler Shough knew he was getting man coverage. The throw vs. man on this concept is THE CORNER ROUTE (the flat by Olave is intended to pull the flat defender away from the corner route, which it did). He found it slightly late, as the timing was thrown off by a good jam at the line — credit the Lions’ defense here. What was absurd to me is that the Lions defender had at least one hand covering Lance’s face while making contact with his body the entire time the ball was in the air. Am I blaming the refs for a loss? No. I am wondering how NFL officiating can have a review overturn an obvious fumble (which changed the outcome) while the refs are clearly afraid to “decide the game” by changing the outcome with a flag.

End of the Day

While the Saints had a sluggish start to the game, especially Tyler Shough, it was undeniable that they displayed a level of fight and belief in their quarterback that hasn’t graced the Black and Gold sideline since Drew Brees was captaining the offense. The film review gave me belief that this is a very talented roster with a smart coaching staff that will have plenty of success throughout the year.

item.title: Davis Webb’s debut as a playcaller was an epic failure
item.description: There was a lot of hype and anticipation about Webb’s debut as a play caller, and well, his debut was an epic failure.
item.content:encoded:
This offseason, Denver Broncos Head Coach Sean Payton did what many people thought he would never do. He handed over play-calling duties to newly hired/promoted offensive coordinator Davis Webb. After being a highly sought-after coach this offseason, Webb returned to the Broncos and was supposed to help the offense take the next step this season. He was going to be more aggressive, bring new ideas, and continue to develop his strong working relationship with quarterback Bo Nix. There was a lot of hype and anticipation about Webb’s debut as a play caller, and well, his debut was an epic failure.

Where do we begin? It looked off from the very first snap. Nix, who has been historically good at avoiding sacks, was sacked on the very first play and was sacked a total of 4 times last night. He would go on to throw an ugly interception to end the opening drive and finish the night with multiple turnovers. Nix played one of the worst games of his Broncos career last night.

Now, let us talk about the run game, or lack thereof. While the Chiefs ran for 220 yards on the ground last night, the Broncos could only muster 61 yards rushing and seemingly abandoned it early on when it was no more than a one-score game. Veteran JK Dobbins was out-snapped by RJ Harvey last night and had just 8 carries for 36 yards.

Remember Jaylen Waddle? They made a blockbuster trade for him during the offseason, spent all of camp hyping him up and talking about how he’s going to change this offense. Remember that guy? He was targeted just 3 times and had 1 catch for 2 yards. Even after the Chiefs lost starting rookie corner Mansoor Delane after the opening-drive INT. Courtland Sutton was targeted 5 times and had 2 receptions for 11 yards. Combined, the Broncos’ top two wide receivers in their new and improved offense totaled 3 catches for 13 yards.

That’s not what you want.

The offensive line was bad too. I haven’t seen the tape, and I am no offensive line guru, but the pressure was getting to Nix throughout the night. Veteran defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo simply out-coached Davis Webb last night.

Now, let’s talk play calls. It’s 3rd and 1 in a close game, and the Broncos go 5-wide? You have a fullback on your roster, paid Adam Trautman to be a blocking tight end specialist, kept Nate Adkins on the roster, and re-signed JK Dobbins (Kenneth Walker was a free agent), and you decide not to run the ball? Meanwhile, the Chiefs faced multiple short-yardage situations and went to their heavy package, dominated the Broncos at the LOS, and converted multiple first downs.

It is just one game, and Webb has been an impressive coach thus far, but there is no beating around the bush on this one. His debut as a play caller was an epic failure. Can he improve? Of course. Teams and play callers have bad games and bad starts to the season. Sean Payton’s teams are known for their slow starts. However, Webb needs to turn things around quickly or else Sean Payton, who looked edgy on the sidelines last night, is going to takeover play calling duties sooner rather than later.

item.title: Ranking best and worst debuts of players, coaches in NFL Week 1
item.description: First impressions aren't always particularly meaningful in the NFL. In Week 1, however, several players and coaches stood out in a new setting.
item.content:encoded:
First impressions aren't always telling in the NFL world.

Week 1 is naturally ripe for overreactions. And after a long summer wait, it can be difficult not to draw conclusions based on how some teams fare in their initial showings.

Of course, the opening week inevitably produces some outcomes that later become exceedingly difficult to square. In 2025, for example, Pete Carroll's Las Vegas Raiders bested Mike Vrabel and the New England Patriots. Any assessments from that game didn't prove meaningful, as the Raiders went on to earn the No. 1 pick and fire Carroll, while the Patriots rebounded and captured the AFC crown.

But even if patience is required, some of the first glimpses of players and coaches in new settings shouldn't be summarily dismissed. And though some of the most anticipated veterans re-introductions were spoiled by injury – including Myles Garrett, A.J. Brown and Kyler Murray – many more warranted a closer look.

With that in mind, here are the best and worst debuts of NFL Week 1:

Best debuts of NFL Week 1

1. John Harbaugh

Even with the excitement of Harbaugh's hire extending throughout training camp and the preseason for the New York Giants, the notion of the former Super Bowl coach bringing a level of respectability to the once-proud franchise on Day 1 seemed far-fetched. Following one of the most impressive all-around displays of the weekend, that no longer seems like a pipe dream.

From tone-setting physicality on both sides of the ball to a distinct level of persistence, the Giants showed in a 28-20 win over the Dallas Cowboys they could live up to Harbaugh's vision of what the team could become in short order. Jaxson Dart exhibited a level of composure not previously seen in his volatile rookie campaign, completing 23 of 29 passes for 230 yards and three touchdowns with no interceptions. New York also pushed Dallas around upfront en route to converting 9 of 11 first downs. While four fumbles and 114 penalty yards left plenty to work on, the Giants showed a resilience that should serve them well for the rest of the season.

Regardless of whether the Giants build on this or suffer setbacks in trying to push for their first NFC East crown in 15 years, flipping the script on what had been a lopsided rivalry served as the ideal start to an already invigorating era.

2. Declan Doyle

Jesse Minter had plenty of believers as a figure capable of engineering a rapid turnaround for the Baltimore Ravens. But while the first-time head coach seemed sure to provide a steady hand, what was less certain was what to expect of Doyle. The 30-year-old, who became the league's youngest play-caller and offensive coordinator, was put in charge of providing a new direction for the offense and rejuvenating two-time NFL MVP Lamar Jackson.

At the very least, Doyle's debut served as proof of concept for his hiring. The Ravens erupted for 41 points in a rout of the Indianapolis Colts that underscored just how creative this attack can be. Doyle deployed Zay Flowers out of the backfield and otherwise seemed to fully leverage his skill set as an undersized speedster who can get a defense on its heels in an instant. The receiver's 150-yard outing was just one of several highlights on a day that saw Jackson recapture his explosiveness as a runner and confidently attack in the dropback game, both from the pocket and on the move.

Reeling off 500 yards every week probably isn't a realistic standard for Baltimore, especially if Flowers and fellow receiver Ja'Kobi Lane are slowed by the injuries that knocked them out of Sunday's game. But there might not have been a more stirring initial showing for a potential contender than the one Doyle strung together on Sunday.

3. Joe Brady

Having been promoted from offensive coordinator to head coach of the Buffalo Bills, Brady was hardly an unknown entity to the team he took over. But in his first game at the helm, the NFL's youngest coach struck a new chord for a franchise demanding a fresh voice.

Facing a Houston Texans team that had a solid claim as the league's most dominant unit, Brady unleashed an aggressive attack that was integral to scoring a 36-31 win. Josh Allen fired 16 of his 29 attempts more than 10 yards downfield and routinely connected. DJ Moore, who could have been a candidate for this list on his own, lived up to his billing as a man-coverage beater in the vertical game, with his threat opening up opportunities for others elsewhere. And Dalton Kincaid was freed up with a heavy dose of motion, allowing him to post the most receiving yards (130) by a Bills tight end since 1967, according to ESPN.

Buffalo's defense left plenty to be desired, but in a league where outcomes are coming to be driven by any imbalance in explosive plays, Brady might be the figure needed to help the Bills push the throttle.

MORE: Bills cracked Texans' dominant defense. Takeaways from wild AFC tilt

4. Kenneth Walker III

Very rarely does a signing as seemingly straightforward as Walker's addition by the Kansas City Chiefs pan out right away. It took all of one game, however, for the big-play running back to demonstrate how far he can carry an offense desperate to re-establish its potency working from under center.

In a "Monday Night Football" triumph over the Denver Broncos that seemed destined to be defined by Patrick Mahomes' return from last December's season-ending knee injury, Walker instead took control. He paced the attack early with 105 scrimmage yards. Not long after halftime, though, his 60-yard touchdown scamper on fourth-and-1 struck the sharpest contrast with Kansas City's offense of the last two seasons. For an attack that had long been hampered by its complete inability to generate any explosive plays on the ground, Walker showed just how capable he is of creating for himself when he bounced left and then sprinted down the sideline to deflate a defense that had overcommitted on the inside.

Denver's uncharacteristically dreadful defensive performance has to be taken into consideration here, with the missed tackles on Walker accounting for half of the Broncos' total, according to Next Gen Stats. But with Kansas City's passing attack still hampered by its lackluster receiving corps, Walker looks on track to be a centerpiece rather than a mere flourish.

JARRETT BELL: Patrick Mahomes wins, Broncos new play-calling plan loses as Chiefs dominate

5. Mike LaFleur

When LaFleur was the penultimate official hire of a coaching carousel that featured 10 vacancies, most envisioned his first year with the Arizona Cardinals as something to merely push through. Waiting in 2027 would surely be a top pick, as well as a war chest with which to acquire the free agents necessary to prop up a spotty roster.

But with a 26-14 win over the Los Angeles Chargers, LaFleur pulled off one of the biggest surprises of Week 1. Though many saw the outcome as a reflection of the Chargers' missteps rather than the Cardinals' achievements, Arizona had plenty going for it. Jacoby Brissett led a composed offense that converted 6 of 14 first downs. The defense, meanwhile, conjured up big plays in critical spots. It might be an outlier result for a franchise still facing a challenging road in the NFC South, but Arizona will take any signs of encouragement it can muster.

6. Isaiah Likely

Amid the unrest about the Giants' shortage of pass-catching weapons, Likely and his value to this offense might have been drastically overlooked.

The mismatch-creating tight end capitalized on the Cowboys' coverage breakdown, powering a win in Harbaugh's debut with his game-high eight catches for 78 yards and two touchdowns. He also kept a methodical offense moving, hauling in four third-down catches for conversions. With New York's passing attack likely having to live in the short-to-intermediate game and middle of the field when not going to top target Malik Nabers, Likely could be in for a substantially high volume of looks on a weekly basis after never topping 60 targets in a season with the Ravens.

7. Raheem Morris

Fans rightly fawned over Kyle Shanahan and a masterful game plan for the San Francisco 49ers in their resounding win over the Los Angeles Rams in Australia. Comparably impressive, however, was how Morris pulled the strings for a defense that took control of the game.

One year after its severely shorthanded pass rush generated heat less frequently than any other unit, San Francisco pressured Matthew Stafford on 44% of his dropbacks. Morris achieved that feat while seldom blitzing, instead throwing the reigning NFL MVP off his game with slants and twists that exploited vulnerabilities in the Rams' front. The 49ers upped the confusion and complexity by sprinkling in dime packages. Coverage, meanwhile, was consistently physical from the line of scrimmage to the catch point. All that created a cascading effect in which the Rams couldn't escape the third-and-long situations that they routinely faced, with just two third-down conversions on the day.

In all San Francisco held Los Angeles to its lowest scoring output (7 points) in any start by Stafford. Morris clearly had a bead on Sean McVay, under whom he served as the Rams' defensive coordinator before taking the Atlanta Falcons' head-coaching job. But this was the kind of performance that should put the rest of the NFC on notice rather than just the Rams.

8. Trey Hendrickson

In his first showing for the Ravens, the two-time NFL sack king didn't get home the way he did at his peak for the Cincinnati Bengals. Even with just one tackle, though, Hendrickson was still plenty disruptive.

Next Gen Stats credited the pass rusher with eight pressures, with half of them coming under 2.5 seconds. There was also a marked difference in the defensive performance when he was on the field and when he was off, with the 58.6% pressure rate dropping to 20% on the snaps he missed. The showing, which Minter called "dominant," was all the more impressive given that it came against a typically stellar left tackle in the Colts' Bernhard Raimann.

9. Jacob Rodriguez

A second-round linebacker's effort in a losing performance might not seem worthy of the spotlight. Rodriguez, however, was a clear standout in the rebuilding Miami Dolphins' loss to the Las Vegas Raiders.

The second-round pick out of Texas Tech notched 14 tackles – the second-highest total of Week 1 – and fared well in coverage. Of course, there was only so much he could do to compensate for an underdeveloped defense's shortage of talent and experience at every level. But as the NFL's only green-dot rookie, he was a persistent and active presence for a group short on building blocks.

10. Anthony Hill Jr.

There wasn't much to like about the Tennessee Titans' initial showing in a 23-10 loss to the New York Jets – more on that later – beyond Hill. Still, the second-round linebacker from Texas at least provided one positive to focus on.

Carrying over a strong training camp and preseason, Hill notched a league-high 16 tackles in Week 1. He also recorded two pass breakups and, if not for a controversial call by an official, could have added a forced fumble and recovery to his output. As a rangy playmaker perfectly suited for Saleh's scheme, Hill can solidify the middle of a defense that still is in search of plenty of support elsewhere.

11. Antonio Williams

Any hopes of the third-round rookie from Clemson making early waves for the Washington Commanders seemed to be dashed when the team signed veteran Stefon Diggs in August. But with the Philadelphia Eagles locking down go-to target Terry McLaurin on Sunday, someone needed to step up for Jayden Daniels to give the offense a chance in a close contest.

Williams answered the call, racking up a team-high 64 receiving yards and a touchdown on four catches despite running just 10 routes. The slot receiver shook free from All-Pro Cooper DeJean for his first catch and displayed sure hands on a 1-yard touchdown pass that Daniels put at ground level. Opportunities might remain limited, but keeping Williams sidelined could be difficult given how few easy answers Washington has at its disposal when McLaurin is guarded.

Worst debuts of NFL Week 1

1. Robert Saleh

Served up a prime opportunity to score revenge against the franchise that jettisoned him, Saleh seemed to have all the elements in place to get his second coaching stint off to a favorable beginning – except, of course, for his own team's performance.

In what might be the opening weekend's most unequivocal failure, the Titans were outclassed in almost every facet. Saleh admitted he was taken aback by the discrepancy between the two teams, both of which were merely seeking some baseline of competence on which to build. New York did a far superior job of establishing that, nearly doubling up Tennessee in yardage (367 to 195) while controlling the contest at the line of scrimmage. Cam Ward and the offensive line alternated turns doing disservices to one another, with the quarterback showing a rare level of resignation on a third-down supposed sack in which he merely walked out of bounds.

The troubling news for Saleh: the degree of difficulty ramps up considerably from here. The next four weeks bring meetings with the Eagles, Giants, Ravens and Texans.

2. Mike McDaniel

Offseason hype, meet regular-season reality. Imagining the Chargers immediately unlocking the full extent of their capabilities under their new offensive coordinator's proven scheme was a fun summer hypothetical. It proved to be just that, though.

Los Angeles' loss to the Cardinals stood out as arguably the biggest letdown for any contender. The explosive running game never took off for the Bolts, and the suspect setup of the interior offensive line proved every bit as problematic as many figured it would. Yet perhaps the biggest issue for the Chargers was an overall lack of cohesiveness between Justin Herbert and his pass catchers. That issue was exacerbated by leading receiver Ladd McConkey's third-quarter exit with a rib injury.

Perhaps operational misfires should have been expected given the intricacies involved in making McDaniel's attack work. Still, next week's tune-up against the Raiders needs to yield substantial progress, as a brutal seven-game stretch awaits on the other end.

3. Christian Parker

Nowhere to go but up from here, right? That was the sentiment that seemed to color the offseason for the Cowboys' defense, which surrendered a league-worst 30.1 points per game in 2025 and routinely unraveled with coverage busts. That still seems to be the prevailing mindset, though, after Parker failed to deliver the level of cohesion he was brought on as defensive coordinator to institute.

With the Cowboys routinely offering up easy gains, the Giants were all too content to take them. Sometimes that meant repeated completions to the flat, where running back Devin Singletary hauled in three completions in four plays to get New York its final score of the evening. Occasionally, it entailed leaving Likely wide open, as Dallas did in the end zone on the first of the tight end's two scores. The end result was enough to spark some postgame furor from typically mild-mannered coach Brian Schottenheimer, who bemoaned the lapses by young players.

Upon his hiring, Parker was touted for his adaptability and later highlighted it as a crucial component of his approach. He'll have to be far quicker to respond if the Cowboys are to turn up the heat and cut down on the mistakes that defined this disappointing first go.

BUMBACA: 'Not our standard': Cowboys have long way to reach Super Bowl expectations

4. Mike Rutenberg

You're forgiven if the name of Jim Schwartz's successor doesn't immediately ring a bell. Rutenberg was tasked with maintaining what Schwartz built for the Cleveland Browns after the celebrated defensive coordinator left the franchise when he wasn't selected as its new head coach. It didn't take long for things to fall by the wayside for the unit.

Cleveland's defense was hardly the only problem in a 34-10 rout by the Jacksonville Jaguars that quickly got out of hand, but this was a jarring outcome for a group that still had several promising pieces. Rutenberg's dramatic scaling back of the Browns' blitz rate, combined with his tilt toward zone coverages, left Trevor Lawrence plenty of room to operate. The quarterback responded by repeatedly attacking the intermediate level while mixing in a couple deep bombs for four scoring strikes total on the afternoon. Defensive end Jared Verse, the core asset in the Myles Garrett trade, was held without a pressure for the first time in his career. Meanwhile, Liam Coen's misdirection and manipulation had reigning NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year Carson Schwesinger out of sorts.

Though it's not time to sound the alarm on the unit just yet, this could serve as a reminder of just how difficult things might get for Cleveland across the board in 2026.

5. Romeo Doubs

This might have been the most notable – and perhaps lone – instance of a high-priced free-agent signing truly fizzling out in Week 1.

Nearly six months after signing a four-year, $68 million deal to help level up the New England Patriots' passing attack, Doubs was essentially ignored in the season-opening loss to the Seattle Seahawks. Despite top target A.J. Brown exiting the game, the former Green Bay Packers receiver earned just three targets and was held without a catch. An ugly drop in the fourth quarter was followed by Drake Maye's second interception of the night.

Doubs admitted he wasn't "locked in enough" on the pass and vowed to be better in the coming weeks. With Brown out at least four weeks and possibly longer, the Patriots need him to help pace a passing attack that's suddenly short on weapons again.

6. Reed Blankenship

A Texans defense that had seemingly everything shored up one of its few weak spots this offseason by adding Blankenship to an already stellar back end. The fifth-year safety was coming off a shaky final campaign with the Philadelphia Eagles, but he looked poised to bounce back after generally holding up well both in coverage and against the run throughout his career.

Against the Bills, however, Blankenship was a significant liability. Pro Football Focus credited him with giving up 110 receiving yards on six receptions. The clear low point came when he tried to undercut an Allen pass to the sideline but instead allowed Moore to coast into the end zone for a 43-yard touchdown. Houston's defense might not stay down for long, but its susceptibility to allowing explosive plays could be a major pain point if Blankenship doesn't settle in better.

7. Rueben Bain Jr. and Alex Anzalone

To combat their defensive downturn, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers spent the offseason addressing two key deficiencies: an edge rush that topped out as passable and a linebacker corps that repeatedly let the rest of the unit down. Substantial investments in both areas didn't move the needle much in a season-opening loss to the Cincinnati Bengals.

The pre-draft questions about Bain's short arms were almost certainly overblown, but the No. 15 overall pick drew a nightmare matchup against massive right tackle Amarius Mims, who engulfed him on almost every passing down en route to holding him without a pressure. And while second-round linebacker Josiah Trotter notched a pick-six and had several encouraging stretches, Anzalone missed multiple tackles and repeatedly came up short in coverage against the Bengals' backs and tight ends, who did much of the heavy lifting.

8. Jaylen Waddle

There was only so much that the Broncos' new wide receiver could do to alter the trajectory of a game in which so many of his new teammates floundered. But any time a game-breaking talent is traded in an effort to put an established contender over the top, coming up nearly empty in the box score warrants mention.

Waddle had just one catch for 2 yards against the Chiefs. Beyond his bare stat line, the receiver also had an unfortunate third-down drop early in the second half. The Broncos had bigger problems, of course, as Bo Nix took four sacks and the run game evaporated. But while buying low on Waddle might be wise, Denver might have to make more of a concerted effort to integrate him into the attack.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Ranking best and worst debuts of players, coaches in NFL Week 1

item.title: PFT's Week 2 2026 NFL power rankings
item.description: The champs hang on, barely.
item.content:encoded:
1. Seahawks (last week No. 1; 1-0): They can win with Drew Lock. It's unknown how long they'll have to try to do that.

2. Bills (No. 5; 1-0): If winning a regular-season game got Joe Brady to take off his shirt, he'll be butt naked if they win in the playoffs.

3. Bears (No. 6; 1-0): The 59 offense is possibly better than the 46 defense.

4. Texans (No. 3; 0-1): Scoring 31 points should be more than enough for that defense.

5. Jaguars (No. 9; 1-0): They won 34-10, and it felt way more lopsided than that.

6. Ravens (No. 10; 1-0): Derrick Henry may never lose a step.

7. Bengals (No. 11; 1-0): In past years, they would have fully blown a 27-10 lead.

8. Chiefs (No. 13; 1-0): Kenneth Walker III earned every penny of his contract in his debut, and then some.

9. Eagles (No. 8; 1-0): A Week 1 escape vs. the Commanders answered no questions about whether they'll be true contenders.

10. 49ers (No. 15; 1-0): They turned the page decisively on all of those bizarre offseason storylines.

11. Rams (No. 2; 0-1): They're already all alone in last place of the NFC West.

12. Broncos (No. 4; 0-1): Maybe they should have tried to get Drew Brees to come back for last night's game, too.

13. Patriots (No. 7; 0-1): Fortunately, blowing it twice in the same game counts as only one loss.

14. Lions (No. 14; 1-0): The Lions had better hope the Saints are destined to be really good this year.

15. Vikings (No. 19; 1-0): For the second straight year, the Vikings woke up just in time to get a key division win in Week 1.

16. Giants (No. 20; 1-0): Jaxson Dart is the real deal, as long as he can stay healthy.

17. Steelers (No. 18; 1-0): For the second time in three years, T.J. Watt personally delivered a win over the Falcons in Week 1.

18. Cardinals (No. 32; 1-0): Jacoby Brissett is better than you realize.

19. Chargers (No. 12; 0-1): Who's got it better than us? Don't ask.

20. Packers (No. 16; 0-1): Matt LaFleur should be very happy he got that extension.

21. Saints (No. 24; 0-1): They may already be the best team in the division.

22. Cowboys (No. 17; 0-1): Like every year, the offseason's delusion gets a hard dose of reality.

23. Panthers (No. 21; 0-1): The Panthers have only themselves to blame for giving the Bears the pick that became Caleb Williams.

24. Buccaneers (No. 22; 0-1): The Browns are the perfect antidote to a Week 1 clunker.

25. Colts (No. 23; 0-1): They get plenty of hype every year, and they ultimately don't deliver.

26. Jets (No. 29; 1-0): Welcome back, Geno.

27. Raiders (No. 30; 1-0): They started 1-0 last year, too.

28. Commanders (No. 27; 0-1): At least they didn't get blown out.

29. Falcons (No. 25; 0-1): Maybe they should have just kept Kirk Cousins.

30. Titans (No. 26; 0-1): It could be another long year in Nashville.

31. Dolphins (No. 28; 0-1): They aren't tanking; they're just not good.

32. Browns (No. 31; 0-1): Prediction — Dillon Gabriel will be the starter by Week 10.

item.title: Deep dive on David Bailey’s NFL debut during Jets win over the Titans
item.description: After showing some promise in preseason, Jets rookie David Bailey made his first regular season appearance at the NFL level and acquitted himself well in the Jets’ 23-10 win over the Tennessee Titans.
item.content:encoded:
After showing some promise in preseason, Jets rookie David Bailey made his first regular season appearance at the NFL level and acquitted himself well in the Jets’ 23-10 win over the Tennessee Titans.

The second overall pick was part of a collective defensive effort that held Tennessee under 200 net yards and limited them to zero plays of 15 yards or longer. Bailey’s debut saw him on the field for 35 defensive snaps, during which he was credited with four tackles, a sack and a quarterback hit.

Let’s dig deeper into how he performed and what this tells us about his potential to develop into an impact player:

First of all, let’s talk about Bailey’s sack, because anyone who watched the game could be forgiven for having missed this. It was initially Will McDonald’s interior pressure that flushed Titans quarterback Cam Ward from the pocket. Bailey then pursued Ward across the field and forced him out of bounds for a 1-yard loss.

While this was an anti-climatic way for Bailey to register his first NFL sack, it was still an important play, as Ward was unable to get down the sideline for a third down conversion, forcing a Titans punt.

This wasn’t the only time Bailey impressively chased Ward down in space after he had vacated the pocket either. He recorded a knockdown on a Ward throw-away after interior pressure came from T’Vondre Sweat on one play and chased across the field to get in his face after his interior rush was repelled on another.

Bailey wasn’t just benefiting from the work of others, though. He also helped set up Kingsley Enagbare’s sack by overpowering a tight end and getting upfield to disrupt what was obviously supposed to be an end around to the dangerous Chimere Dike. With Bailey in the backfield, Ward couldn’t make the pitch to Dike and was sacked as he tried to step up.

In all, Bailey registered pressure on Ward several times and, although he didn’t really beat his man cleanly on any of these, he was clearly a handful as he moved his man off his spot a few times and got upfield well with outside leverage on a few other occasions.

Bailey was primarily matched up with former first round pick JC Latham, the Titans’ right tackle, until late in the game when he got more reps on the right side. To Latham’s credit, he was doing a good job of re-routing Bailey upfield whenever he tried to rip through around the edge. However, even on these occasions, it was often squeezing the pocket sufficiently to force Ward to step up.

In addition to drawing a holding penalty on Latham, Bailey’s best rep may have been with the Titans backed up near their own end zone as he went speed-to-power and got Latham moving backward, then disengaged to chase Ward out of the pocket. Ward was able to avoid being sacked for a safety but Bailey was able to force him out of bounds for a 5-yard gain.

While he was clearly disruptive as a pass rusher, Bailey’s long-term future will depend just as much on his ability to play the run. Due to the Titans being unable to sustain drives, Bailey was only in the game for six run snaps but he held his own on those for the most part and was in on the tackle on three of them, although he only officially got credit for two.

The six plays went for 30 yards, although 10 of those came late in the game when Bailey was standing up on the edge, basically conceding easy yardage with the Jets in prevent mode. Otherwise the only negative play he had saw Latham drive him 2 yards off the line and seal him inside to set up an off-tackle run for positive yardage. Good linebacker play by Demario Davis and Jamien Sherwood limited that to a 5-yard gain though.

One other under-the-radar contribution Bailey made came on a run up the middle that went for a 6-yard gain in the third quarter, which speaks to his versatility. Bailey was initially lined up on the edge, but the tight end went in motion so he dropped off into the box and was 4 yards off the line of scrimmage at the snap.

As Tony Pollard hit the hole cleanly and broke out to the second level, Bailey made a solid form tackle in the open field to bring him down. While that play perhaps didn’t have a high degree of difficulty, it was definitely important because if Bailey missed that tackle, Pollard would have had 10-15 yards of green grass ahead of him.

On a day when the Titans’ longest play was only 14 yards, the importance of Bailey preventing a chunk play that could have started to swing the momentum back in Tennessee’s favor cannot be understated, especially since he made the play while doing something that is not his primary role.

On the whole, the Jets will be extremely encouraged by Bailey’s first game. While he’s yet to flash dominance, the fact that he is already being productive is an excellent sign. Expectations will be high that he can build on this on Sunday against the Packers and in the games ahead.

item.title: The Hot Read: Josh Allen doesn’t care about your asterisk
item.description: Josh Allen is clutch - deal with it.
item.content:encoded:
Kamari Lassiter should have caught it.

That became the immediate rallying cry for the many naysayers of Josh Allen following the Buffalo Bills’ incredible win over the Houston Texans. In a game that featured eight lead changes, Buffalo took the lead for the final time with just over a minute remaining in regulation when Allen hit Josh Palmer on a frozen rope down the seam for his second touchdown pass and fourth total score of the day.

The play before, Allen threw a pass that seemed to come on a miscommunication with Palmer. The veteran receiver turned left, the ball went right, and Texans cornerback Kamari Lassiter had a chance to make a play on the ball and potentially end the game. He stumbled, the ball bounced out of his hands, and the Bills’ drive continued.

“Lassiter should have caught it.” Well guess what? He didn’t. You know what else Lassiter should have done? Not commit pass interference in the end zone to set up an Allen rushing score. He also shouldn’t have allowed Palmer to get open on the very next play after the dropped interception for the game-winning score.

For that to be the sole focus for so many, as if every other quarterback in the NFL doesn’t get those type of lucky moments, is purposely turning a blind eye in order to drive home a preconceived narrative – a narrative that lacks any merit whatsoever.

Allen had four total touchdowns and 334 yards passing against the league’s top defense and didn’t turn the ball over once. In the fourth quarter, he went 7-of-12 for 122 yards and the aforementioned touchdown to Palmer. Yet there are still those who will swear to you that Allen isn’t clutch.

Since 2020, of the 46 quarterbacks who have played at least 300 snaps, Allen has the highest EPA in the fourth quarter and overtime out of all of them. Additionally, since 2022, of all quarterbacks to play 150 snaps, Allen has the highest EPA per play when trailing, and his 209 impact plays lead the NFL in that time span – no other quarterback has more than 184, per Sumer Sports.

It’s only one game, but it was the type of game the Bills are rarely on the right side of. This time, in the first game of the Joe Brady era, Allen had an EPA per play of 0.48, which ranked third among all quarterbacks who played 25 snaps in Week 1 and was second in impact plays in a building that had become his personal hell house over the last two years.

So sure. The Bills had a bit of luck on their side in the waning moments of Week 1 – something they’ve had positively none of in the Allen era in the biggest games. Perhaps this is a sign that fortune will finally favor the Bills – that requiem will be replaced by rapture. In 20 weeks time, we’ll know for certain.

That’s the cold open – this is the Hot Read.

Three and Out

Chiefs remain major AFC threat, Broncos remain fraudulent

So it turns out that, despite the largely hopeful projections from those picking the Chiefs to miss the playoffs, Andy Reid and Patrick Mahomes are still pretty good. Kansas City annihilated the Denver Broncos 31-10 to close out Week 1 on Monday night, with Kenneth Walker arriving in a big way. The reigning Super Bowl MVP rushed for 173 yards and put up two touchdowns to help lift the Chiefs’ offense over a Denver defense who struggled to bring down ball carriers all night.

Denver missed 19 tackles throughout the course of the game. Per Trevor Sikkema, the Broncos accumulated 248 missed tackle yards, which is the most in a single game in the NextGenStats database. The Chiefs leaned on Walker and rookie Emmett Johnson, as well as the legs of Mahomes to carry an offense whose passing game was largely anemic all night. The Chiefs’ 220 yards rushing were the third-most for an Andy Reid-led team.

Far too many were singing ding dong the witch is dead as it pertains to the Chiefs. 2024 was a year that featured unprecedented luck for Kansas City, which was followed by a year of nearly unfathomable bad luck in 2025. 2026 will split the difference. Will the Chiefs win 15 games? Almost certainly not? 11 or 12, though? Why can’t they?

In terms of Denver, I didn’t pick them to make the playoffs for a reason – their quarterback is a liability. Bo Nix finished the night 17-of-28 for 131 yards, one touchdown and an interception thrown on his first pass of the season to rookie Mansoor Delane. His 4.68 yards per attempt were 31st in the the league, ahead of only Cam Ward and his 4.38 mark. On top of that, Nix had an average depth of target of 3.85 yards – the lowest of any quarterback in Week 1. Jaylen Waddle was supposed to give Denver an added ability to push the ball downfield – he finished the night with one catch for two yards on three targets.

We touched on the Chiefs having terrible luck in 2025, well the Broncos had an unsustainable amount of good luck, winning 12 one-score games – that isn’t going to happen again. Having one of the league’s top defenses and leaning on that unit is all well and good … until that unit has a bad night and you don’t have the quarterback and offense capable of picking up the weight that was put down.

The Chargers are still the Chargers

The first job of any kind I had covering the NFL began in February, 2020. I was a junior at Slippery Rock University. Every year that I’ve covered the league, I’ve had to listen to a not-small-number of my colleagues go on their respective platforms and say, “I tell ya what, I really like the Chargers this year.”

In that span, the Chargers have the same amount of playoff wins as I do. And entering Week 1 of the 2026 season after another offseason of metaphorical eyeball emojis following the hire of Mike McDaniel at offensive coordinator along with Jim Harbaugh all but declaring Justin Herbert to be the one true God of Earth, the Bolts entered their season opener agains the Arizona Cardinals as the heaviest favorites of the week (9.5 point favorites, per FanDuel Sportsbook). How did they back up all the hype? They lost by 12 to a Cardinals team largely projected to be drafting in the top five come April.

Justin Herbert finished the week 23rd in EPA per pass, and before you launch out the evergreen offensive line excuse, he was pressured on just 28.6 percent of his dropbacks, which was the third-lowest of any quarterback form Week 1. When it came to late-down passing, Herbert had a success rate of just 11 percent, which ranked 30th in the league, only ahead of Bo Nix and Deshaun Watson.

Let’s go ahead and cut to McDaniel’s presser later this week when he’s wearing goofy glasses and mumbling through every question like a 15 year old stoner who just figured out how to make a bong by hollowing out an apple while watching Rick & Morty. The schtick got old in Miami, and it’s going to get old very quickly with the Chargers.

T.J. Watt shows change was needed for Steelers

For years, if you dared to suggest that the Pittsburgh Steelers should move on from Mike Tomlin, no fewer than three dozen people would hit you with the same phrase: “He would get hired in five minutes if the Steelers fired him.”

So many assumed that Mike Tomlin was the straw that stirred the drink for the Steelers, and that he was the lone reason for their three consecutive 10-win seasons from 2023-25. However, the play of T.J. Watt in Week 1 would suggest that Tomlin was holding back the Steelers more than he was pushing them forward.

Following what was the worst season of his career, notching just seven sacks, Watt began the 2026 season with arguably the best game of his career. He sacked Cooper Rush twice, had three tackles for loss, and all but put the game away with his first career pick-six.

What was so different about this game than any other in the last number of years for Watt? His usage. Watt played in just 38 snaps – something that was unheard of under Tomlin when he was on the field for just about every play every week. Mike McCarthy and defensive coordinator Patrick Graham made it a point to rotate their edge rushers and keep them fresh, and that strategy paid dividends in Week 1.

Not only did the Steelers keep Watt clean, they moved him around the defensive line – something that just didn’t happen under Tomlin and former defensive coordinator Teryl Austin. He played on both the left and right side, registering a sack on each side, and overall, the Steelers’ defense finished the week second in defensive EPA per play.

And it’s not just the defense that looked refreshed, the offense pushed the ball downfield. Aaron Rodgers’ 24-of-40 box score won’t blow anyone away, but the Steelers left a lot of meat on the bone in the explosive department. Roman Wilson had a deep touchdown slip out of his hands, and DK Metcalf had multiple drops and an offensive pass interference that negated big yards. Overall, 104 yards on the drops and OPI were kept off the board. Had those plays gone the Steelers way, Rodgers finishes the day with north of 300 yards and two touchdowns.

Despite that, his average depth of target was 10.49 – higher than any game he played in 2025 by over a yard and sixth in the league overall. He also led the NFL in deep pass attempts with nine. Pittsburgh is becoming more modern on both sides of the ball – that wasn’t going to happen under Tomlin.

One play that changed everything

How about Bills defensive tackle Deone Walker? The massive 6-foot-7, 331 pound defensive tackle registered six tackles and two tackles for loss, but the biggest play of the Bills’ win over Houston was Walker’s sack in the game’s final seconds.

After C.J. Stroud completed an 18-yard pass to Jaylin Noel to give Houston 1st-and-goal at the nine, Walker busted through the middle of the Texans’ offensive line to sack Stroud. Houston had to burn its final timeout, and instead of having two more shots at the end zone from inside the 10 and a timeout in their pocket, they were pushed back to the 18 yard-line with no timeouts. Two plays later, Greg Rousseau had a strip sack that was recovered by Terrell Bernard to seal the game.

Buy or sell

Buy: Trevor Lawrence

After an incredible second half of the 2025 season that saw Trevor Lawrence finish fifth in MVP voting, the former No. 1 overall pick continued where he left off last season. He went 18-of-23 for 245 yards and four touchdowns – nearly as many touchdowns as incompletions with a QBR of 93.4. Yes, it was against the Browns, but Lawrence and the Jaguars did what they were supposed to do against a bad team – they dominated.

Sell: Todd Monken lasting more than one season

Monken has already announced that Deshaun Watson will start in Week 2, and the fact that we are somehow on Year Four of this is nothing short of remarkable when it comes to this franchise’s incompetence. This is another hopeless season for Browns fans that becomes even more perilous for Monken with every game that Watson starts.

Buy: Declan Doyle

The Baltimore Ravens’ new offensive coordinator wasted no time leaving his imprint. In his first game calling plays, Baltimore put up 506 yards of offense and 41 points on Lou Anarumo and the Indianapolis Colts defense. Lamar Jackson connected with Zay Flowers five times for 150 yards, while Derrick Henry racked up 144 yards and three touchdowns on the ground.

Sell: Packers ability to finish

Green Bay has now cumulatively lost its last six games, and they have majored in soiling themselves in the fourth quarter in their last two games. In Week 1 agains the Minnesota Vikings and the wild card round against the Chicago Bears, Green Bay held second half leads of the combined score of 43-13 and found ways to lose both games. A failed fourth-down conversion while up 22-17 in the final minutes of the third quarter is where things began to go south. Instead of taking the field goal and going up by eight, the Vikings took over and scored a touchdown nine plays later to take a 25-22 lead. Green Bay turned the ball over on their next two possessions, both of which led to Vikings touchdowns. After holding a 22-10 lead in the third quarter, the Packers allowed the Vikings to score 29 second-half points to run away with a game that looked lost early on after Kyler Murray was knocked out of the game with a head injury.

Buy: Bears offense

How about 552 total yards and 59 points for the Chicago Bears in Week 1? You’t think that when a team scores almost 60, the passing stats would be crazy, but it was the run game that truly went off for Chicago, as they totaled 291 rushing yards and six touchdowns on the ground. Ben Johnson said he wanted the Bears to break the all-time scoring record. Well, that’s a terrific way to start that journey.

Sell: Bears defense

On the flip side, the Bears’ defense looked as bad as I was assuming it would. Chicago made Bryce Young and Jalen Coker look like Steve Young and Jerry Rice, with Young putting up 361 yards and three touchdowns and Coker going for 8-138-2.

This is especially concerning, considering Young ranked 31st in success rate among all quarterbacks with at least 100 dropbacks last season. His 361 yards are his second-most in a game in his career, and the three touchdowns tied a career high.

When mediocre teams and quarterbacks are doing that to your defense, imagine what the great offenses will do. I can respect the insanity of Ben Johnson just trying to outscore his problems, but the Bears defense will be what keeps them from making the postseason in 2026.

Prediction to track

Steelers will trade Joey Porter Jr

The Steelers’ rising star didn’t partake in training camp, and he didn’t suit up in Week 1 after not securing a long-term extension in Pittsburgh. The Steelers don’t negotiate in-season because they operate like a pizza shop in small town, USA, and it has been reported that they are open to trade offers. A team like the Detroit Lions or Washington Commanders would make a lot of sense here.

item.title: Will Aaron Donald suit up for Rams on Monday?
item.description: The Los Angeles Rams have to gear up for Week 2, Aaron Donald questionable for Week 2, and more news on a Tuesday!
item.content:encoded:
Will Aaron Donald make his 2026 debut on Monday Night Football against the New York Giants? The Rams may need him. With Myles Garrett out, and the entire team looking middle of the pack (at best) against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 1, the Rams may need Donald to help them get back in the win column.

It’s not time to panic, but it is time to seriously realize that if the Rams do not start stacking wins now, or at the very least show some improvement in Week 2, this season could get away from them quicker than they had ever considered.

It’s Tuesday, time will tell who all will be officially active on Monday night. Could Donald be one of the Rams to come out of the tunnel? Stay tuned.

Rams HC Sean McVay noncommittal on Aaron Donald’s Week 2 status (ramswire)

“Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay isn’t tipping his hand on whether Aaron Donald will suit up for Monday Night Football against the New York Giants, saying the Rams simply haven’t made a decision yet.

“He’s going to continue to work his process,” McVay said, “and we’ll see what that looks like.”

Sean McVay offers positive updates on 3 Rams injuries (ramswire)

“McVay called the updates on safety Kam Curl, inside linebacker Nate Landman, inside linebacker Omar Speights and tight end Davis Allen “positive,” suggesting the Rams could get some of their key contributors back sooner rather than later.

Curl exited Thursday’s game in the second half with an ankle injury. While he was officially listed as questionable to return, McVay said the veteran safety “is good,” downplaying the injury as ankle soreness. Curl has quickly become one of the most important pieces of the Rams defense, starting all 17 games last season while playing 99% of the defensive snaps. He signed a $36 million contract extension this offseason. Jaylen McCollough replaced Curl after going down, who had two tackles before exiting.“

4 things Rams learned from Sunday’s games: Are LaFleur’s Cardinals…good? (ramswire)

“As always in the opening weekend of the season, there were plenty of surprises and new developments across the league. Here are four things the Rams learned about their foes in the NFC, including a couple of impressive upcoming opponents in the Cardinals and Giants.

Cardinals won’t be the easy out many people expected them to be

The Cardinals’ projected win total was set at 3.5 before the season started. After just one game, they’re already a quarter of the way toward eclipsing that number set by oddsmakers. They beat the Chargers convincingly on Sunday, 26-14, in Mike LaFleur’s head coaching debut. And they were on the road in L.A., too.“

Did Browns Know More Than Rams Ahead of Myles Garrett Trade? Why Deal Timing Was Perfect (heavy.com)

“Garrett earned his second Defensive Player of the Year award in 2025 after tallying 23 sacks and breaking the NFL’s single-season mark in that category. He wanted a raise heading into his age-31 campaign and didn’t make sense for Cleveland’s timeline, given the Browns don’t appear likely to have a true franchise QB before 2027, which probably means it will be at least 2028 before the team can seriously contend.

The Browns executed a deal with the Los Angeles Rams, after which Garrett missed considerable time during the spring and summer with knee issues that included swelling. Now, after one wildly underwhelming performance in a blowout loss to the San Francisco 49ers in Australia, Garrett is going to miss at least four weeks due to surgery.“

Reeling Rams defense can’t afford to underestimate Jaxson Dart and the Giants (ramblinfan)

“While 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy picked apart the Rams, the Giants’ Jaxson Dart dominated the Cowboys secondary in similar fashion, completing 23-of-29 passes for 230 yards and three touchdowns. He was cooly efficient en route to averaging an impressive 0.73 EPA per play, wasting little energy in leading his offense to a touchdown in every quarter.

And now the LA defense, which is already reeling, must step up and stop him in Week 2.

Rams defense won’t be overconfident vs Giants in Week 2

Whatever exposed the Rams so badly, those factors have been scrubbed for Week 2. They are no longer anointed as default winners. The roster is no longer seen as bursting with insurmountable superstars, many of whom either struggled in the season opener, are injured entering Week 2 (i.e., Myles Garrett),or both.“

Texas A&M Legend Myles Garrett’s Injury Situation Takes New Turn (sports.yahoo)

“Myles Garrett‘s highly anticipated debut with the Los Angeles Rams did not go according to plan, and now the former Texas A&M star is facing a significant absence after undergoing knee surgery.

Garrett was dealing with the knee issue throughout the summer, limiting his participation during training camp and the preseason. However, the Rams believed the veteran defensive end would be able to manage the injury and contribute once the regular season arrived.“

Rams tumble in Week 2 power rankings: Is LA a top-5 team? (ramswire)

“5. Los Angeles Rams (1): Woof. At least you couldn’t blame the special teams for this loss? But the Rams scored their fewest points of the Matthew Stafford era, while WR Puka Nacua had more tackles (1) than ballyhooed offseason acquisition Myles Garrett, who will be out at least the next month – apparently he should’ve stayed in L.A. with Aaron Donald. This was likely an anomalous defeat, if a reminder that the Lombardi Trophy is guaranteed to no team.“

Rams undecided if Donald will play vs. Giants (nbcsports)

“Donald was kept off the Week 1 roster for last week’s opener against the 49ers, and the Rams did receive a two-game roster exemption for Donald after he agreed to return. Speaking on Monday, McVay said Donald will “continue to work his process” and that the team will see how things look from there. With the Rams losing Myles Garrett (knee) for at least the next four games, it’s safe to assume they would like to get Donald on the field sooner rather than later.

– Zachary Krueger”

Broncos-Chiefs on ‘Monday Night Football’: What We Learned from Kansas City’s 31-10 win (nfl.com)

“Davis’ Denver offense stymied. As Patrick Mahomes made his much-ballyhooed return after tearing his ACL and LCL last season, his former Texas Tech teammate Davis Webb was making his debut as the Broncos play-caller and offensive coordinator. Monday went much better for Mahomes. Webb and Broncos QB Bo Nix, in his first game since breaking his ankle in the Divisional Round, never found any consistent success.  Kenneth Walker’s 191 total yards for the Chiefs bested the Broncos’ 176. Nix looked sharper earlier passing than Mahomes, but it made no matter as the game wore on with Denver shockingly held to nine first downs and its ground game non-existent. J.K. Dobbins was the leading ground gainer with a meager 36 yards, while Nix’s 19-yard TD toss to Evan Engram to tie the game in the first quarter was really the last splash of any kind had by Webb’s offense. After the Chiefs vaulted ahead, 21-7, on a stellar 60-yard gallop by Walker in the third quarter, Mahomes was picked off by Brandon Jones on the Chiefs’ ensuing drive. Set up at the KC 5-yard line, Nix and the offense went backward and settled for a 31-yard field goal by Wil Lutz — Denver’s last points of the game. With such high expectations and such a disastrous debut for Webb and the offense, one has to wonder how long head coach Sean Payton will wait until snatching the offensive reins back.“

NFL ties Week 1 scoring record for Super Bowl era (nfl.com)

“Thanks to the Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos combining for 41 points on Monday night, the opening slate of games for the 2026 season has officially tied the 2012 season’s record for the most Week 1 points scored (791) during the Super Bowl era.

Entering Monday’s AFC West showdown, teams had averaged 50.0 combined points per game, per NFL Research, with the Week 1 finale bringing the average down to 49.4.“

Comment of the Day:

“McVay, I like you as a coach, I’m proud to say you’re the coach of the Rams. But why try and see if he can “play through” with his knee issue? He could have had the knee surgery in late July and been ready by now.?I think you and Snead were embarrassed to admit it, tried to cover up the knee issue after this big trade that’s why you wanted to see him “play through” it. Of course you or other coaches wouldn’t you traded for damaged goods.

It is what it is. I’m not coach or GM. You now have to deal with a rough schedule, let’s see how you guide the team through it. It’s one game but I think not just physically but the players were mentally tired thinking boy these Niners were here for a week and well rested while our team tried to shuffle through a long flight with little sleep. Please don’t do that again.“ -LaRams&NyMets
