item.title: NFL Week 2 power rankings: 49ers behind Rams despite Week 1 win
item.description: Are the Niners the best team in the NFL after 1 week?
item.content:encoded:
We had a fun NFL slate wrap up in blowout fashion on Monday night, as the Kansas City Chiefs beat the Denver Broncos 31-10 to cap a memorable Week 1. There were some timely upsets, some close battles, and then some blowouts between good teams.

Kansas City had one of those games. The San Francisco 49ers had another when they beat the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 back on Thursday night in Australia, marking one of the best Week 1 wins on the slate (if not the best).

Heading into the season, the 49ers were viewed as the clear No. 3 team in the NFC West. After one week, they arguably look the strongest, with the Seattle Seahawks dealing with an injury to quarterback Sam Darnold.

Week 2 power rankings in the NFL were released by several publications on Tuesday morning. Let’s take a look at where the 49ers rank among the pack.

ESPN: No. 5

San Francisco jumped up four spots from No. 9 to No. 5 in ESPN’s Week 2 power rankings, although they remained third in the NFC West. Here’s the top five teams on their poll:

1. Buffalo Bills

2. Seattle Seahawks

3. Baltimore Ravens

4. Los Angeles Rams

5. San Francisco 49ers

Despite the win over the Rams, the 49ers remained one spot behind them in the rankings. They also remained behind the Bills, who beat the Houston Texans 36-31 on the road in a thriller, as well as the Seahawks and Baltimore Ravens.

While the Seahawks (No. 2), Bills (No. 3), and Rams (No. 1) were all in the preseason top-five, the 49ers (No. 9) and Ravens (No. 8) both made considerable jumps after Week 1.

The Athletic: No. 1

The Athletic’s Chad Graff and Josh Kendall wasted no time anointing the 49ers at No. 1, pointing to their offense after the 27-7 beatdown last Thursday.

“After the franchise’s drama-filled offseason and with questions about the aging roster, the 49ers had no trouble moving the ball against the Rams. Brock Purdy threw for three touchdowns, the running game (including rookie Kaelon Black) looked good and Raheem Morris’ defense was great. It’d be hard to draw up a better start.”

Here’s how the top five looked:

1. San Francisco 49ers

2. Seattle Seahawks

3. Buffalo Bills

4. Chicago Bears

5. Baltimore Ravens

The Rams fell from No. 1 to No. 6 here, followed by the Kansas City Chiefs, who jumped from No. 14 to No. 7.

FOX Sports: No. 7

Despite the marquee win, the 49ers didn’t move considerably here in FOX Sports’s power rankings, jumping just three spots from No. 10 to No. 7. Here’s all the teams ahead of them.

1. Baltimore Ravens

2. Chicago Bears

3. Seattle Seahawks

4. Buffalo Bills

5. Los Angeles Rams

6. Cincinnati Bengals

All of these teams were ahead of the 49ers in FOX Sports’s preseason power rankings.

“They heard all the talk about the dream team Rams and became L.A.’s worst nightmare. If the Niners stay healthy, they actually could end up the best team in the dangerous NFC West,” FOX Sports’s Ralph Vacciano wrote.

USA Today: No. 2

The 49ers jumped up five spots in USA Today’s power rankings up to No. 2, trailing only the Seattle Seahawks, who beat the New England Patriots in the season opener without Sam Darnold.

“Their “Sleep tight” tweet served as the mic drop of Week 1 after the Niners, who were at least close to full strength after juggling so many injuries in 2025, stuck it to the apparently jet-lagged Rams in Australia,” USA Today’s Nate Davis wrote. “The NFC West is already shaping up as a three-way heavyweight bout once again, and the Niners − if healthy − have certainly shown they’ve got the goods to be a Super Sunday threat.”

Behind them were the Buffalo Bills, Chicago Bears, and Los Angeles Rams.

The Niners definitely surprised most in Week 1, having strong play to go in the trenches to support their well-rounded team. Things are a lot different in Week 2, as they’ll host the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, where they’re already a massive 13.5-point favorite.

item.title: Lions scouting report: Can Bills reach Super Bowl?
item.description: Diving into the Buffalo Bills heading into their Week 2 game against the Detroit Lions.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time this season, the Detroit Lions hit the road, heading to Orchard Park, New York, to face the Buffalo Bills. The Bills have a brand-new home in Highmark Stadium, and what a game to open it, primetime on “Thursday Night Football.“

Detroit is coming off an overtime thriller at home against the New Orleans Saints, needing a stop on a two-point conversion to win. Buffalo defeated a tough team in the Houston Texans in a shootout on the road. Both teams are top Super Bowl contender in their conferences, and this game is a rare good game for a Thursday night.

This could be a statement win for whoever comes out on top. If Detroit wins, they are moved up the chain as a threat in the NFC. If Buffalo wins, they’ll reinforce the belief around the league that they’re the team to beat in the AFC. Let’s dive in on the Bills and see why they’re the toughest team on the Lions’ schedule this season.

Buffalo Bills

2025 Season

  • 12-5 record (2nd in AFC East)
  • 4th in points for, 12th in point allowed
  • Overall DVOA: 8th (4th on offense, 20th on defense)

2025 was a slight step back for the Bills compared to 2024, as they lost to the Denver Broncos in overtime in the AFC Divisional Round. In 2024, they reached the AFC Championship Game, where they lost to the Kansas City Chiefs. The team, once again, failed to live up to the offseason hype, and their inability to reach the Super Bowl despite the talent on the roster cost their head coach, Sean McDermott, his job afterward.

Quarterback Josh Allen was coming off his MVP season in 2024, and while his stats were similar to the year before, he was sacked the most times ever in his career: 40. Allen threw for 3,668 yards (11th in the league) with 25 touchdowns and 10 interceptions. His success on the ground continued, as he rushed for 579 yards and 14 touchdowns, averaging 5.2 yards per carry.

Speaking of running the ball, Allen got a big help in running back James Cook, who led the NFL in rushing yards with 1,621, a career high. He also found the end zone 12 times and averaged 5.2 yards per carry. His ability to move the rock between the tackles helped take some of the weight off Allen’s shoulders, who had previously had to do all the heavy lifting. It also strengthened their read-option play calling, as teams accounted for Cook more than Allen.

For the passing game, Allen struggled to have a dominant top receiver on the team, as Khalil Shakir led the team in catches (72) and yards (719), but only scored four touchdowns. The touchdown leader was tight end Dalton Kincaid, who got 39 catches for 571 yards and five touchdowns.

Defensively, the Bills didn’t really stand out in anything particular. EDGE Joey Bosa was one of their top contributors, getting five sacks and leading the league in forced fumbles with five. EDGE Gregory Rousseau led the team in sacks with seven, and safety Cole Bishop led the team in interceptions with three and tackles (85). Buffalo had the 17th-ranked passing defense and 12th-ranked run defense per DVOA, so that side of the ball wasn’t their best, and they relied on their offense to win games.

2026 offseason

Key additions: EDGE Bradley Chubb, CB Dee Alford, S Chauncey Gardner-Johnson, WR DJ Moore (trade)

Key losses: G David Edwards, EDGE Joey Bosa, EDGE A.J. Epenesa, CB Cam Lewis, HC Sean McDermott

2026 NFL Draft picks

Round 2: EDGE TJ Parker
Round 2: CB Davison Igbinosun
Round 4: OT Jude Bowry
Round 4: WR Skyler Bell
Round 4: LB Kaleb Elarms-Orr
Round 5: S Jalon Kilgore
Round 5: DT Zane Durant
Round 7: CB Toriano Pride Jr.
Round 7: P Tommy Doman Jr.
Round 7: G Ar’Maj Reed-Adams

Buffalo did more addition than subtraction, starting with the firing of McDermott. With McDermott gone, the Bills promoted offensive coordinator Joe Brady to head coach. On the defensive line, the Bills needed veteran help and upgrades, and they believe they got some. While losing Epenesa to free agency and Bosa to possible retirement, the Bills signed Chubb to a three-year deal worth $43.5 million. The secondary got some help as well, getting cornerback Dee Alford and former Lions safety Chauncey Gardner-Johnson.

The Bills’ biggest loss was guard David Edwards, and losing two veterans on the defensive line forces them to shake things up there. Cornerback Cam Lewis was the biggest loss in the secondary for Buffalo. The Bills addressed most of their losses in the 2026 NFL Draft, taking EDGE TJ Parker and cornerback Davison Igbinosun in the second round. The Bills gave up one of their second-round picks for Chicago Bears wide receiver DJ Moore, giving Allen a boost in the passing game and a clear WR1 for the team.

The rest of the draft was for depth purposes, snagging multiple offensive linemen and secondary players, while getting a new punter as well. Overall, the Bills roster doesn’t have as much turnover as other teams, with the biggest change at head coach. They believe they are close to winning a Super Bowl, so I get the few moves they made.

2026 season thus far (1-0)

Week 1: Defeated Houston Texans, 36-31

Stats:

  • 5th in points scored, 22nd in points allowed
  • Overall DVOA: 4th (2nd on offense, 23rd on defense, 3rd on special teams)

What a game to start the year for the Bills; going on the road and defeating the Texans isn’t easy. The Texans’ defense is tough, and the Bills needed to score on their final drive to win and put up 36 points. Allen had a solid game, throwing for 334 yards and two touchdowns, rushing for 23 yards on six carries and scoring two more times. Cook was limited most of the game, rushing for 57 yards, averaging 4.4 yards per carry, and had three catches for 12 yards.

Allen didn’t take long to find success with his new weapon in Moore, as he finished with five catches for 100 yards and a touchdown. Kincaid finished as the leading receiver with five catches for 130 yards, and wide receiver Joshua Palmer found the end zone on his only catch for 34 yards.

Defensively, the Bills had a rough day in slowing down the Texans offense, allowing quarterback C.J. Stroud to throw for 274 yards and two touchdowns. While Stroud played well, former Lions running back David Montgomery led the charge, rushing for 60 yards and two touchdowns while also catching three passes for 19 yards and a touchdown. If the Texans needed to score, they gave the ball to Montgomery.

The Bills forced two fumbles and recovered both; one turned into a field goal early in the game, and the last came on the final drive, leading to the Bills kneeling it out. Rousseau finished with two sacks, and both fumbles were caused by him, making him the most impactful player on the defense on Sunday. If not for his big day, the Bills might have lost the game.

Injury notes

Key players ruled out: None

Key players to monitor: DT T.J. Sanders (knee), RB Ty Johnson (hamstring)

Injuries haven’t really affected the Bills much at the start of the year. Defensive tackle T.J. Sanders and running back Ty Johnson missed Week 1, but both could potentially play in Week 2 (both listed as limited on Monday). Johnson is dealing with a hamstring injury, but it appears the team held him out to get him ready for Week 2. Sanders is dealing with a knee injury after popping up on the injury report late last week, and Brady downplayed the severity of the injury, saying he missed last week as a precaution.

Biggest strength: Quarterback

Facing off against a former MVP in Allen, it’s hard not to see him as the team’s biggest strength. The offense runs through Allen overall, and without him, this team wouldn’t be the same. Allen isn’t your typical dual-threat quarterback; the man acts like a bulldozer while running with the football. Allen isn’t afraid of contact like most quarterbacks, and his agility is impressive for someone his size.

He’s got a massive arm, and he hopes to use it more this season with Moore available to throw to. If he were a pocket passer, then there would be room for debate on him being the biggest strength, but with a solid running back in Cook, Allen forces defenses to choose who they want to go after. Allen makes you pay no matter which direction you go and is a game-changer for the Bills.

Biggest weakness: Secondary

The team’s biggest weakness so far is its defense. With the defensive line getting three sacks, along with the run game holding the Texans to an average of 3.9 yards per carry, the finger can’t be pointed at them. The secondary struggled with Stroud and his receivers, as starting wide receiver Nico Collins had seven catches for 75 yards and a touchdown.

While the Lions only threw for 206 yards and two touchdowns against the Saints, it could’ve been more if wide receiver Jameson Williams didn’t have a rough game. He dropped multiple passes, and quarterback Jared Goff threw a few risky throws. The passing offense for Detroit is much tougher than Houston’s, with two solid receivers, a tight end, and a running back that can all be an option at any given moment. If the Bills’ secondary can’t make a play or slow them down, it could be another shootout.

Key matchup: Lions defensive line vs. Bills offensive line

Last season, Allen was on his back more often than he’d like. With the Bills losing a starting guard in Edwards, it’s not looking likely that things will improve that much with little changes made to the line. Enter the improved Lions defensive line. With the Lions’ defensive line being their strong suit on defense, they are going to be after Allen all game long. The question is, can they contain him if they can get to him?

Allen will make some plays; he’s one of those players that you just have to accept will get theirs. If the Lions can generate enough pressure on him quickly, though, he won’t have time to make many of those plays. The Lions’ defensive line is at their strongest with no injuries, and defensive tackle Alim McNeill is back to his old ways after recovering from his ACL tear in 2024.

Against the Saints, the Lions generated 29 pressures and got five sacks, according to PFF. Against the Texans, the Bills allowed 13 pressures and two sacks. The Texans’ defensive line is one of the best, so it’s a good sign so far for Buffalo that they can hold their own. If the Bills can keep that up, the Lions’ secondary might repeat last week, but if Detroit can generate pressure and cause problems, Buffalo’s offensive line might regress to its 2025 form.

Vegas line for Sunday: Bills favored by 4.5

item.title: Cowboys Week 1 fallout: 6 possessions and a funeral
item.description: The Cowboys coaching staff had a poor plan last week.
item.content:encoded:
What a bunch of horse manure. Sorry for such a vivid description, but organic soil fertilizer is the only way to accurately capture the aroma of the broken spirit of this Cowboys fan. After months of begrudgingly building up excitement for this Dallas Cowboys football team, this is our reward. Maybe a little of that’s on us, but they get us every time. Every. Time.

And losing to the New York Giants? For perspective, we’re talking about a football team that hasn’t won 10 games in a single season since Dak Prescott was a rookie. A team so traditionally incompetent that they usually secure a top-10 draft pick, miss on a defender, and then rinse and repeat the following year. We count on those games for wins and confidence boosters.

But this current Giants team is pretty good, which is a painful thing to type. Especially since they’re so hateable. Cam Skatteboo looks like a high school bully from an ’80s movie who hangs out with his Cobra Kai buddies. And his headbutt compatriot, Jaxson Dart, is equally nauseating. His arrogance is so insufferable that John Harbaugh had to get on him during practice because he was taunting his own teammates. Rivals or not, these guys are remarkably easy to hate.

But who cares about the stupid Giants? The real, existential dread today comes from the Cowboys. There is plenty of blame, but the coaching staff will be the recipient of our complaints today.

The new season began with two horrible plays that went nowhere. A one-yard stuff of Javonte Williams, and an incomplete pass intended for CeeDee Lamb. Just like that’s it’s third-and-long against the one thing the Giants defense can supposedly do well. Rush the quarterback. The Cowboys answer with a quick slant to George Pickens in what looks like a drive-sustainer, only replay shows he was just inches short of the first-down marker.

No problem. Just sneak it. We all were thinking it. They’re at their own 37-yard line, but if you can’t get a few inches, you might as well just pack this thing up and head back to Texas. Let’s GOTI this thing already!

Nope. Instead, they subject us to that embarrassing pre-snap charade where they are trying to get the Giants to jump offsides. So annoying. Please stop doing that. First possession of the year – THREE. AND. OUT. Yay!

Why am I whining about one silly possession? Well, because the Cowboys only had six of them on the night. As it turned out, each one was pretty important. We’ll get to the why in a minute, but if you look at the Cowboys’ offensive possessions, it went like this…

Punt

Punt

Touchdown

Interception

Touchdown

Touchdown

Note: We aren’t counting the three-play possession with only 14 seconds left in the first half. Instead, let’s focus on the six real possessions.

There are two interesting things about this list. First, the Cowboys scored a touchdown on half of their possessions in the game. If teams do that, they’re usually going to light up the scoreboard. That’s a lot of touchdowns. But when they only get six total chances, half isn’t as rewarding.

Equally as aggravating as the lack of opportunity was the grueling labor required for the Cowboys offense to move the ball. Nothing came easy. There was little creativity. Running back Javonte Williams had to fight for every inch, usually first running into the back of his own blockers. Dak Prescott had to deliver a lot of tight throws, and their most explosive chunk plays on the night came courtesy of pass interference penalties.

Okay, enough dumping on the offense. Let’s switch it up.

The Cowboys defense was terrible on Sunday night. For starters, they couldn’t stop the run. The defense allowed 165 rushing yards in this game, the most rushing yards they’ve allowed since Week 8 of last season when the Denver Broncos ran all over them. You remember that game. It was awful. That’s what we got on Sunday night.

Instead of Christian Parker’s new scheme confusing the quarterback, the quarterback repeatedly confused them. Dart had them faked out all night, with defenders running the wrong way, and playing the chase game 10 yards down the field. It was terrible.

About the only thing worse than their inability to stop the run was their coverage scheme. It’s hard to know exactly what the issue was, but watching the Giants’ receivers wander so comfortably in wide-open spaces was tough to witness. That was not the defense we signed up to watch. We saw that last season.

Frustration continued as we sat back and essentially watched none of the new guys make an impact. Rashan Gary? Von Miller? Did those guys play?

Caleb Downs had a nice play where he sacked Dart that would have stood out more if the ball didn’t flutter right into the hands of a Giants’ offensive lineman, but other than that, it was a quiet night from the team’s new safeties. Even the well-anticipated aggressiveness of rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham ran himself into an encroachment penalty on a crucial third and short. Fantastic.

Everyone knows there will be growing pains with a new defensive coaching staff. It’s expected. Even so, there are still things you are hoping to see. We didn’t see them.

This is only one game, and nobody should be running for cover as if the sky is falling. It’s not. Again. It’s just one game. But it was a terribly coached game. The team looked completely unready for the season and repeatedly committed the silliest infractions you can do in a football game. Offsides (twice), holding, illegal hands to the face. Pure silliness. And many of them came on crucial third-down situations. The coaches had to waste a precious second-half timeout when they only had 10 players on the field. It was pure sloppiness. There’s no other way to explain it.

For the Cowboys, this is a tough one to swallow for a very simple reason. They just weren’t ready to play. Letting an opposing offense control the entire game to the point where they only got two second-half possessions was utterly painful to watch.

The team must get their act together, and get it together quick. They suddenly find themselves in a crucial game against the Washington Commanders next week. If they drop another one, they’ll head to Baltimore, where they could likely start the season 0-3. And remember, the first half of the season is the easy part. Things get really difficult come November.

item.title: Dolphins Week 1 review: Thoughts and reactions from Raiders loss
item.description: I think I thought I thought what I thought.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time in 16 years, I do not have NFL Sunday Ticket.  The good news is that NFL+ has a condensed version of the game, so I can skip a lot of the talk and in-between play stuff that the normal podcast.  I can watch kickoff to final whistle in about 45 minutes.  The bad news is that I can’t watch live via that source.  I say all of this to preface the fact I watched the game LATE Sunday night, and that process will not likely change this season.  With weekends being what they are for me, all my immediate takes will be from the perspective of watching the game late and trying to remember everything I saw.  So if things seem off, perhaps that’s why.  Perhaps.  Anyway, here we go.

Youth and experience was front and center

This has been THE major talking point all offseason and we all knew coming into this season that rookies were going to play a major factor.  This Miami Dolphins team is loaded with players who have not played many NFL snaps on both sides of the ball.  Profootballreference.com has the snap counts and starters from the game on their site.  On offense, Miami started 3 rookies: Caleb Douglas, Will Kacmarek, and Kadyn Proctor.  On defense, Miami started 3 rookies: Jacob Rodriguez, Chris Johnson, and Michael Taaffe.  The Douglas, Kacmarek, and Proctor played 51, 14, and 56 snaps respectively, with 56 being all the offensive snaps. Rodriguez, Johnson, and Taaffe played 68, 68, and 51 snaps respectively, with 68 being all the defensive snaps.  Other rookies like Chris Bell, Kevin Coleman Jr., and DJ Herman saw significant snaps.

But it wasn’t just the rookies.  There were several starters who have limited playing time at the pro level.  Starting safety Zayne Anderson played 53 snaps yesterday, which represents over 25% of his career total.  Malik Willis, whom I highlighted as an “experienced rookie” played 56 snaps, which represents about 10% of his career total.  Jordan Phillips, Jason Marshall Jr., Dante Trader Jr., and Zeek Biggers are all second-year players who played significant snaps against Las Vegas that all have less than 500 NFL snaps in their careers.

That’s a long-winded way of saying the Dolphins are about as wet behind the ears as they can be across the board.  That is going to lead to sloppy play from everyone.  There are going to be missed assignments.  There is going to be miscommunication.  I saw more than one occasion where the offensive line looked more confused than the defense. 

There is going to be a lot of splintery wood to sand down before this looks like what we want it to be.  That doesn’t make it any easier to watch, but it does add some perspective when you realize that of 22 starters, only 8 had more than 1000 career snaps entering this contest.

Coaching is a concern

I read something somewhere that this game was only like the 6th time in NFL history that 2 rookie head coaches faced off against one another.  Maybe that’s true; maybe it’s not.  What I can say is that one set of coaches looked like they knew what they were doing and the other did not.  The Raiders are not a good team and they know that.  They have limited weapons and an older QB that is only there as a bridge for their rookie.  That coaching staff knew that and did what any good coaching staff would do: protect their QB and let their one top playmaker carry the load.  And by protect their QB, I mean get the ball out of his hands and don’t let him do stupid stuff.  One might look at Cousins’s stat line and see 21-30 and 3 TDs.  But he only threw for 160 yards on those 30 attempts.  A high completion percentage and low YPA means what class?  That’s right… Captain Kirk was Captain Checkdown.  I don’t blame them one bit.  They were smart to lean on the running game.  They were smart to target a rookie cornerback – and Cousins is savvy enough to do that.  When Cousins did look downfield, it was usually bad. He had a few completions.  He also completed a few to the Dolphins.  Cousins wasn’t particularly good this game despite his stat line looking somewhat nice.  That team just played smarter and looked better coached.

To counter that, the Dolphins didn’t sell out to stop the run.  Or maybe they did.  I don’t remember.  It was late.  But I would have had 8 in the box at all times and forced Cousins and limited pass catchers to beat me.  Only one WR on the Raiders had a YPC average over 10 and that was because he caught the one decent downfield throw from Cousins. But no… the Raiders ran over the Dolphins and ran over them some more.  It was a disappointing showing from a defensive calling standpoint.  Now, I will give Hafley a slight break… typically offensive head coaches have an advantage over defensive head coaches starting out.  But Hafley will need to improve.  If he is going to sink or swim with rookies and green players, he might as well go all out with them.

On the flip side (hat tip to WZB), Miami’s offense was like that annoying card player at the poker table that goes all-in every hand.  Everything was a run or deep pass.  I saw a screen pass or two, but that was it.  No checkdowns, no easy passes, no “drive starters.”  I recall the Raiders having several plays where Cousins threw a quick out for a 4-5 yard gain at most.  Where was that for Miami?  That’s how you protect your quarterback.  That’s how you stay on schedule and maintain proper down and distance. I get the game script got out of hand late, but the play calling was very suspect (also hat tip to JUK – I was preparing this before I read his post, so make sure you read it).

This and that

  • Caleb Douglas may be for real.  I’m going to be a little hesitant because the Raiders don’t exactly have a shutdown secondary. But a “reach” in his debut game going 5-94 on 7 targets is nothing to write off.  He should only improve. Sully may have struck gold here.
  • Kadyn Procter looked ok out there.  Perhaps an All-22 review is in order.  I saw a player who missed several assignments, which is a communication issue. That’s not necessarily a rookie mistake, but the 1st team OL has been the same from day one. That’s something that should be mitigated by now.  I also saw Achane get dropped for a loss because Proctor got obliterated.  A 360 lbs. OL should NOT get pushed THAT far back on a run play.  That is simply unacceptable. But he also had some good run blocks and held up decent in pass pro.  OL reviews really require All-22 film and the condensed replay doesn’t rewind the easiest (on the TV anyway), but from what I could see, he had good and bad moments.
  • Malik Washington can be a reliable target for Willis, but if he is used the right way.  McDaniel had him running sweeps and behind the LOS kinda stuff and that’s good.  But Slowik has a 6’4” and 6’2” receiver at his disposal and he’s running deep sideline routes to a 5’8” WR?  Come on now.  This comes back to the play-calling.  Putting Washington in position to catch the underneath stuff and use RAC skills will best fit what he can do AND give Willis the needed “easy pass” option.
  • Malik Willis was… ok.  I don’t think he played poorly overall, but there were some issues that need to be addressed.  Aside from the playcalling aspect, he took some bad sacks.  Before fans jump on the “oh noes, the OL sucks again”, this is very likely ALWAYS going to be a part of Willis’ game.  He is going to hold the ball longer than we have seen under the previous regime.  Yes, some of it was poor blocking.  Let’s give the Raiders some credit.  They have one of the game’s best pass rushers in Crosby and edge rushers Kwity Paye and Malcolm Koonce are solid players.  But Willis is going to take sacks that his predecessor never would because of how he plays.  Play-calling can also help with the sack numbers.  Getting the ball out quickly became a standard thanks to the McDaniel era, but it is a tool that most good play-callers use to their advantage.  Willis also provides the rushing element that Miami has never truly had outside of an occasional run from Ryan Tannehill.  Still, he made some good throws, and I think the overall game script just got away from him.  I believe he tried to play some hero ball and he really didn’t need to do that.
  • Maybe the safety room isn’t ALL that bad.  Ok, they were out of position some and missed some tackles.  But they also made some plays.  Taaffe had 4 tackles and an INT and SHOULD have had a forced fumble.  Trader had 3 tackles and an INT.  Anderson had 5 tackles, a TFL, and a PBU.  There is talent here.  How quickly can it come together?
  • Speaking of Anderson’s PBU, that “taunting” call… that’s weak sauce.  That was potentially a momentum-shifting play.  The Dolphins had given up a score and then gone 3-and-out.  The pressure was on the defense to get a stop and they did.  But because Juju Brents stood near an opponent and made the “incomplete” sign, that’s a penalty?  Get ALL the way out of here with that.  Unless he said something to the player, which didn’t appear to be the case, that’s a horrible call for a silly infraction.  It was a big hit that jarred the ball loose, and he got a needed stop.  He celebrated with his teammate, and because the opponent was nearby, it was “taunting”. No Fun League indeed.
  • Kenneth Grant is sorely missed.  He may not be the interior pass rushing specialist worthy of a high first round pick yet, but he is a solid run defender at worst.  The run defense was gashed, and his presence would have made an impact.  The fact DE Clelin Ferrell was elevated from the practice squad and not DT Mazi Smith for THIS game was… puzzling.  That goes back to the coaching decisions.
  • Special teams was special indeed.  Patterson missed a 41-yard field goal.  Pinion’s 45.8 yards per punt and 37.0 net yards per punt are 23rd in the league after one game.  The coverage units were atrocious, allowing a 2nd worst 17.5 yards per punt return and absolute worst on yards per kick return at 47.5.  The next worst is Jacksonville at 38.0, nearly 10 yards less per return.  The Dolphins allowed the 2nd best average starting field position to the Raiders, who started on their own 36.9 yard line on average.  On a positive note, the Dolphins averaged 17.0 yards per punt return, which is 3rd best and 6th in yards per kick return at 32.4.  The Dolphins are 8th best in terms of starting field position at their own 33.5, but that is likely buoyed by the 2 INTs, which allowed them to start in or near Raiders territory.

I said what I said

I’m going to try to put on my optimist hat for a moment and tell you that everything will be ok.  It’s a VERY inexperienced team and there were some positive moments that came from this loss.  I also know that I made a bold prediction about wins last week.  But the most concerning part of this game is a potential cause-and-effect.  Being bold is nice and fun to write, but being realistic is looking at the schedule and not seeing a potential win until week 7 against the Jets.  Even though they looked feisty, albeit against a team in the Titans that may be worse than the Dolphins.  This Dolphins team is nearly a 2-TD underdog against the 49ers.  We haven’t seen Kansas City yet (as of when I’m actually writing this), but the Dolphins will not be favored in that game, even at home.  They go on the road to Minnesota, who managed to whip Hafley’s former team at home pretty soundly with a backup QB.  Their starter went down with a concussion and may or may not be available in the Dolphins game.  That could be a factor, but it’s not likely to be a win.  The Bengals will be favored in Week 5.  Coach Hafley said not to measure success in wins and losses this season, and it looks like there will be nothing but losses for the foreseeable future.

That’s the cause of the possible unfortunate effect, which very well could be another one-and-done head coach for the Dolphins.  Coaches generally don’t survive going 0-fer.  I expected the Dolphins to be rough this week but still be able to pull out a victory.  They weren’t particularly close.  The good news is that no one can measure development after one game.  We should expect tighter communication in the next game and then the next.  We should see incremental improvement. If we don’t see it by about midseason, that’s a problem.  The bad news is even if they do improve a little, that it may not be enough.  The wild card factor is new CEO Daniel Sillman.  We don’t know how much control he has over the decision-making process.  Stephen Ross has been rather patient with coaches and staff.  Sillman may not be.  There is twitter speculation that the decision to give season ticket holders free jerseys may be getting rid of backstock due to a potential jersey change.  That may be nothing and may be completely irrelevant, but if he’s wanting more “new and fresh”, keeping a 0-1 win head coach may not be his idea for that.

I’m not saying that Hafley WILL be out, but we’ve seen this movie before.  Miami wanted to clear payroll and start over before.  They hired a defensive head coach that struggled putting together an offensive staff and even with 2 winning seasons, he was ousted.  For Hafley, there needs to be significant improvement.  I don’t expect it this week against SF or even next week against KC.  But they must look like a team that can fight for a win by season’s end.  The 2019 team went into New England in week 17, with New England playing for playoff positioning, and got a win.  The 2026 team needs to show improvement like that, because right now, I’m not confident they can even score. I’m not trying to be an alarmist, but if the one-and-done scenario happens, good things don’t normally follow.  Instead of GM-HC synergy, you get power struggles and conflict.  It’ll be even worse if Sillman decides for “splash” and goes for a known coach like Mike Tomlin. It’ll be deja vu all over again.  Things will go south much quicker and much easier than it starts to turn around.  We need to see more this week, even if the opponent is tougher.  If the same sloppy play, mistakes, and coaching issues could be a bad sign for Hafley.

I know what this season is, so I’m not gonna complain. But I’m tired of failed rebuilds after failed rebuilds and I would like to see one go right. Game one provided more questions than glimmers of hope.

But enough of that ranting… enjoy some greatness to brighten the rest of your day!

item.title: Cowboys poach RB Tyler Goodson off Falcons practice squad
item.description: The Falcons lose their veteran RB3 to Dallas.
item.content:encoded:
Looking for some good news? Well, too bad.

The Falcons lost Tyler Goodson, who was a productive runner and receiver this summer and was the team’s de facto third running back, to the Dallas Cowboys. Because Goodson was on the practice squad, Dallas was free to pluck him and did so to help out their thin running back corps. The Falcons now have just two running backs on the roster—one of them is Bijan Robinson, to be fair—and Cash Jones on the practice squad as depth.

The Falcons knew they were taking a chance with their roster construction, which saw them only keep Bijan and Brian Robinson Jr., but probably didn’t expect to lose their veteran insurance this quickly. The team will almost certainly be calling up Zacch Pickens or Zach Harrison off the practice squad to replace Da’Shawn Hand, who may be lost for the season, and will therefore be able to easily add a player. The problem is that the player they add is unlikely to be as well-rounded as Goodson, who did a nice job this summer and offers you plenty as a runner, receiver, and returner.

Look for former Brown Jerome Ford, who overlapped with Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees in Cleveland, and special teamer/capable receiving back Travis Homer as potential free agent additions. I doubt the Falcons will go very long without adding to the room.

We wish Goodson well, but it sure is a bummer to lose him.

item.title: 5 things we learned about the Chiefs from Week 1 win over Denver
item.description: What did we figure out about this year’s Kansas City Chiefs in game 1?
item.content:encoded:
Well, that was fun. For all the fawning and saddle-riding the national media gave the Denver Broncos heading into this season, it turns out the burros were the paper champions all along.

This game was a good old-fashioned AFC West beat down. Andy Reid and the Kansas City Chiefs dragged the NFL’s angriest little elf behind Arrowhead and took a switch to their backsides like my grandma did when I stole her pack of smokes as a kid.

The Chiefs came out on a mission. They didn’t just want to win this game. They wanted to stake their claim back on the division. This was the Chiefs saying, time to get off the porch, lil pup; the big dogs are back.

And although it’s just one win. It was a heck of a win, as the Chiefs force-fed Denver’s defense the rock like a kid who doesn’t want to eat their veggies at dinner time, rolling to a three-touchdown victory, winning 31-10.

Here are five things we learned from the Chiefs dominating the donkeys.

1. Chiefs can be a running team if they want to be

The Chiefs made a point out of the gate to establish the run come hell or high water, and luckily they didn’t have to wait long for the benefits to take effect. Kenneth Walker was everything he was advertised as and more. Rushing for 173 yards on 23 carries, including an electric 60-yard touchdown run on 4th down.

Do I think the Chiefs will run the ball this much each week? I honestly don’t. But they can if they need to. If left tackle Josh Simmons is going to miss extended time. Or if the wide receivers struggle to create separation. I think there will be weeks where quarterback Patrick Mahomes passes for 300 yards and four touchdowns, but on the days when it’s not there, it’s good to know you can run the ball down the throat of one of the NFL’s best defenses.

2. Mahomes’ knee is fine

Whether they will admit it or not, fan bases all around the NFL were hoping and praying that Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes would be limited in his first return to action since tearing his ACL last season. Because then there was at least a possibility that he would play like a mere mortal.

But those hopes were dashed right off the back, when Mahomes tucked that ball and scrambled up the middle, scoring the team’s first touchdown of the season.

In the words of the man himself, “You woke up the wrong mother******.”

3. Who said you can’t teach an old dog new tricks?

They say you can’t teach an old dog new tricks. Well, it depends on the dog. If that old Saint Bernard is Andy Reid and you’re a competitive son of a buck who doesn’t want the final years of his legacy to be known as a guy who couldn’t change and adapt in the NFL.

By running the ball 31 times, Andy Reid proved on Monday night that all he cares about is winning, and he is willing to change his stripes to get there. But Reid has never been afraid to evolve when the moment called for it. I don’t think this is any different. This is a coach leaning into his offense’s strengths and trying to offset the fact that he has an undrafted rookie starting at left tackle. It was a master class by one of the greatest to ever coach the game.

4. Kahlil Benson isn’t great, but he battled

At times, the pass rush beat him. There were times he looked overwhelmed. But overall, the undrafted rookie free agent offensive tackle played passable football in his first NFL action. If the Chiefs’ regular starting left tackle, Josh Simmons, is going to miss significant time, then the Chiefs will be counting on Benson to hold things down until Simmons can return.

The biggest question now is: how does Benson adapt now that there is an entire game of tape on him out there? You can believe that defenses are watching his reps, and his success will depend on how he responds to their counterpunch.

5. This team is going to be hard to pass against

The severity of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane’s injury hurts this defense. He is a special talent who looks like a cornerstone you can build around for years to come. But even without Delane for most of Monday night, the Chiefs secondary locked down Denver’s vaunted wide receivers, holding Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton to three receptions for 13 yards.

Do I think this performance was an outlier?

Nope.

Fellow cornerbacks Nohl Williams and L’Jarius Sneed were all over the place, too. Now, I don’t think Bo Nix is anything special. But our defense might be. There is a good possibility that our defense is the reason we win games this year.

item.title: 3 OT prospects the Titans already have to know after brutal Week 1
item.description: The Tennessee Titans are clearly going to be in the market for an offensive tackle in the 2027 NFL Draft
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans could not protect quarterback Cam Ward in Week 1. The sophomore top overall selection was under routine pressure in Sunday’s 23-10 loss to the New York Jets. Ward was pressured on nearly 70 percent of his dropbacks, according to Pro Football Focus.

Ward actually did a pretty nice job navigating that pressure. He was only sacked on three occasions, and two of them were decisions to eat the football because nobody was open. Nonetheless, the Titans’ offensive line was putrid.

The tackle play was especially bad from Dan Moore Jr. and JC Latham. They allowed two pressures apiece. Moore was beaten badly around the edge by Will McDonald IV for the third sack on Ward. 

The way-too-early indication is that the Titans will be in the market for at least one new starting offensive tackle next offseason. Possibly with a very early selection in the 2027 NFL Draft. With that in mind, we’ve identified the three offensive tackle prospects the Titans already need to be familiar with.

Trevor Goosby, Texas

Trevor Goosby was excellent at protecting Arch Manning in Texas’ Saturday’s stunning come-from-behind victory over Ohio State. Goosby possesses the prototypical length for an offensive tackle and displays incredible play strength on a snap-by-snap basis. He especially generates so much power as a run blocker, and effectively uses that power and length to keep the edge protected in the passing game.

Jordan Seaton, LSU

Jordan Seaton transferred to LSU this season from Colorado. Through two weeks, he’s handled the step up in competition in flawless fashion. Seaton looks like a natural in Lane Kiffin’s offense. He’s an extremely athletic blocker who thrives in space thanks to high-level foot quickness.

Trevor Lauck, Iowa

Death, taxes, and Iowa producing offensive lineman. Trevor Lauck is the next blocker in the Hawkeyes’ rich history. A mature tackle prospect, he’s technically sound and smart on tape. Think Peter Skoronski, but at tackle. Lauck isn’t an elite athlete, nor does he have elite length, but his skill set is just so technically advanced.

item.title: NFL Panic Meter: Cam Ward had a disastrous performance to start his second season
item.description: Cam Ward and the Titans had a horrible performance in Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
Cam Ward was bad as a rookie. In most measures, he was worse than J.J. McCarthy last season. Nobody paid it much mind.

The Tennessee Titans didn't play a single standalone game, which helped keep Ward's struggles in the shadows. Those who broke down his play chose to single out impressive highlights and blame the situation around him for a poor season. And it was a poor situation. Ward deserved a pass. But that was with the expectation that a new coaching staff and an upgraded supporting cast would lead to better results.

It's hard to judge anything one game into an NFL season. But a season doesn't offer many better opportunities than facing the New York Jets at home when the talent around you is healthy and fresh for the opener. And Ward was just as bad as he was last season.

Through the first nine possessions of the game, which spanned 55 minutes, the Titans had one field goal, one fumble and seven punts. They had seven first downs, 130 yards and trailed 23-3. Ward had 140 passing yards and that looked a lot better because of one garbage-time drive. He got 57 of his yards and his only touchdown on that drive, after the Jets had practically moved onto next week.

There was also one comical rep in which Ward flipped the ball to himself on a trick play. You can do things like that when everything is going well. This one ended with a quick sack.

Let’s check in on Cam Ward pic.twitter.com/U3S05pIKKh

— big ounce (@_bigounce) September 14, 2026

"I am very disappointed," Ward said, via the team's site. "We are better than what we showed offensively. We trained a lot this offseason, we had some hard days. It didn't pay off for us today, but it is going to pay off for us eventually, whether it is next week or the week after. We are going to get it rolling."

Are they going to get it rolling? While the Jets have improved on defense, they allowed the highest passer rating in the NFL last season and were 32nd in defensive DVOA. Again, it won't get easier for the Titans or Ward. And they did practically nothing on offense. Next week the Titans host the Eagles and their stellar defense. It could be ugly.

On Sunday, Titans fans booed. First-year head coach Robert Saleh was asked if he had a message to fans who might be apathetic about the team already, just one game into the season. Maybe it's too early for that, but it seemed like the same Titans from a season ago. The coaches changed, many teammates changed. The quarterback remained the same. As did the results.

It's too early to give up on the No. 1 overall pick after 18 starts, but there needs to be some positive signs, and soon. There haven't been any yet. Ward struggled in the preseason — Titans beat writers said Ward did look good in practices — and that poor play carried over to Sunday. Other than draft pedigree, there aren't many tangible reasons to believe in anything better coming up. That's a tough place to be one game into your second season.

Panic meter: Too early to jump ship on Ward, but not too early to be seriously concerned.

Drake Maye's bad stretch

Nobody is trying to say Maye has played well lately. The three interceptions he threw in the New England Patriots' opener were awful. But the criticism of Maye on social media has gone overboard.

Going back to the recent postseason, Maye has had five subpar games in a row. Those games came against the Chargers, Texans, Broncos and two against the Seahawks. The Texans, Broncos and Seahawks have top-five defenses and the Chargers were a top-10 defense in DVOA last season. Half of one, against the Broncos, was played in a blizzard. There were also factors around Maye that weren't great, whether it was the struggling offensive line last season or injuries to A.J. Brown and TreVeyon Henderson in Week 1 this season. But it has become easy and trendy to shred Maye and call him a fraud, so here we are.

Maye had a fantastic 2025 season. It was against an easy schedule in NFL terms, but it's still pro competition. He didn't play in the MAC. He played well enough to deservedly come one vote from winning NFL MVP. He's 24 years old. Maye is and will be fine. He needs to play better than he has lately. Not playing an elite defense every week should help.

Panic meter: Not nearly as much as you'd think, based on social media pitchforks.

Colts get blown out

The Colts were one of the NFL's darlings in the first half last season, getting off to a great start and being one of the league's best offenses until Daniel Jones tore his Achilles. There wasn't a fast start this season. They lost 41-23 to the Ravens. According to RotoWire, teams that lose by 14 or more points in Week 1 make the playoffs just 18.8% of the time. And losing at home in Week 1 by any margin is a bad sign. Only 21.8% of home Week 1 losers make the playoffs, compared to 29.5% of road losers according to RotoWire.

And it's not just the leaguewide trends. The Colts didn't look good in the opener. Their defense allowed more than 500 yards. Jones had the fourth-worst adjusted EPA (expected points added) per play among all Week 1 quarterbacks. There was never any guarantee Jones would bounce right back after a major injury, and his Week 1 performance was alarming. He had just one run for 4 yards. He didn't pass it well. Nothing looked easy. In a season that is critical for head coach Shane Steichen and general manager Chris Ballard, in terms of their job security, this was an awful start.

Panic meter: Maybe the Ravens are just that good, but the Colts couldn't have been much worse.

Chargers get blindsided

Look away, survival pool players. The Chargers' 26-14 loss to the Arizona Cardinals wasn't shocking just for the loss itself, but how uncompetitive the Chargers were in the game.

The Cardinals clearly outplayed the Chargers. They outgained Los Angeles 393-268. They had more first downs and a better yards per play. It was a 12-point win and that wasn't fluky.

Before being too concerned about the Chargers, remember that odd things happen in Week 1. The Patriots lost to the Raiders at home last season and won the AFC. The Seahawks lost to the 49ers at home and won the Super Bowl. Three of the last 10 champions were 0-1, according to RotoWire.

Teams to start 0-1 that made the 2025 playoffs...

• Seahawks (won Super Bowl LX)
• Patriots
• Bears
• Texans
• Panthers

Teams to start 1-0 that missed the 2025 playoffs...

• Raiders (#1 overall pick)
• Cardinals
• Buccaneers
• Colts
• Commanders
• Vikings
• Bengals

— NFL Researcher (@NFL_Researcher) September 8, 2026

The Chargers looked poor on both sides of the ball. For now, we'll assume this was the weird Week 1 result we'll be talking about months down the road.

Panic meter: A bad loss, but this seems like a one-off result.

item.title: Vikings Crush Packers: Flores’ Blitz, Wentz’s Relief, and the Murray Question
item.description: Vikings dominate Packers, but Murray's concussion clouds the outlook. Film breakdown with Tyler Forness.
item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Vikings demolished the Green Bay Packers in Week 1 — but lost Kyler Murray to a concussion on the 11th play. Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano break down the film, the blitz, and what’s next.

Tyler Forness opened with a bold comparison: “If you remember Enron in 2001, Vikings just did the reverse, where they started out in the dumps and they were riding high on the stock market.” After Murray’s concussion — he was fencing on the field, a telltale sign — Carson Wentz entered and steadied the offense. “Wentz wasn’t the reason for the turnaround,” Forness clarified. “But he was the reason why the ship didn’t sink.” The defense, meanwhile, was suffocating. Brian Flores blitzed Jordan Love relentlessly — and it worked. “Every single one of Jordan Love’s passing yards came against the blitz,” Forness noted. “He was 0 for 5 with a clean pocket.” Dave Stefano compared Flores’ approach to boxing: “B-Flo is almost being a prize fighter… body blows will wear you down quicker… and then comes the knockout punch.”

Key Points:

  • Kyler Murray’s concussion: Murray showed fencing signs and entered the protocol. He was symptom-free and in meetings Monday, but Forness cautioned: “Concussions are weird, and they hit everybody differently.” Carson Wentz is the likely starter Sunday at Chicago.
  • Carson Wentz’s relief effort: Wentz delivered what Forness called “one of the best throws I’ll probably see all year” — a two-point missile to Justin Jefferson. His arm talent kept the Vikings afloat when everything could have capsized.
  • Dallas Turner’s breakout: Seven of 10 pressures were quick (under 2.5 seconds), with a 27.2% pressure rate per PFF. “Lo and behold, it only took him one game,” Forness said, answering critics who said Turner only produced cleanup pressures.
  • Flores’ blitz-heavy dominance: Flores sent five-plus rushers almost exclusively. Jordan Love had no answers — 0 for 5 when not blitzed — and the pressure compounded as the game wore on.
  • Defensive line depth paying off: Jalen Redmond, Levi Drake Rodriguez, and Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins — Kwesi Adofo-Mensah’s 2024 cutdown-day bet — delivered key plays at roughly $2.4 million combined. “Kwesi deserves his flowers for that move,” Forness said.
  • Big Citrus stops Love: Caleb Banks (Big Citrus) stuffed Jordan Love on a pivotal 4th down — with no tush push. “You run at the rookie,” Banks said. Forness added: “The dumb part was not having anybody to help push him.”
  • Will Fries struggles: The guard whiffed on multiple blocks, including the blown assignment that triggered Murray’s interception. “He’s got a lot to prove,” Forness warned, noting a near-$20 million cap hit.
  • Theo Jackson’s bad angles: Jackson took poor pursuit angles repeatedly. “Theo Jackson shouldn’t be playing. He shouldn’t be on the field.”
  • J.J. McCarthy’s status: No beat reporter asked about McCarthy at the presser, which Forness said “tells us everything we need to know about where J.J. McCarthy is currently in this organization.”
  • Looking ahead: The Vikings travel to Soldier Field to face Caleb Williams and the Bears.

item.title: Cowboys add another running back to the active roster
item.description: Cowboys acquire a new player for the roster
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys are continuing to add to the running back position. Before Malik Davis went down with season-ending hip surgery in practice last week, the team had already added Emari Demercado via waiver claims after training camp. Then, after Davis was placed on injured reserve, they signed Israel Abanikanda from the practice squad to the active roster.

Now it looks like the Cowboys will be signing Atlanta Falcons running back Tyler Goodson from their practice squad, per Aaron Wilson. Goodson started his NFL journey as an undrafted free agent with the Green Bay Packers in 2022, but saw his first career snaps after signing with the Indianapolis Colts in 2023.

He spent the next three seasons there and only eclipsed 100 rushing yards in a season once. Goodson joined the Falcons this offseason and had a few standout preseason moments, particularly against the Colts.

Looking at the way Goodson broke free for the touchdown run, his running style looks very similar to what Dallas had in Malik Davis. Maybe the team views Goodson as a better replacement for that skill set than someone like Abanikanda.

Stephen Jones says talent acquisition is 24/7, 365, and adding Goodson shows Dallas was looking to upgrade after what they saw against the New York Giants Sunday night, when the backups to Javonte Williams didn’t perform well.

There’s no information yet on the corresponding move for the Cowboys to sign Goodson to the active roster.

item.title: NFL ties post-merger record for most Week 1 points with Kenneth Walker's late TD in Chiefs' win over Broncos
item.description: The NFL experienced an offensive explosion in Week 1. Is it a fluke or a sign of things to come this season?
item.content:encoded:
Offense was the name of the game in the NFL in Week 1 to the tune of a league record.

After a historic first NFL Sunday in terms of points scored around the league, the Chiefs and Broncos went into Monday night with a chance to push the league over the top for a new NFL record.

They didn't quite reach new heights. But with Kenneth Walker III's touchdown and ensuing extra point to extend Kansas City's lead to 31-10 early in the fourth quarter, the total point tally for Week 1 reached 791 across 16 NFL games. That calculates to a combined average of 49.4 points per game.

That total and that average tally are tied for Week 1 in 2012 for the most points scored in the NFL's opening week since the AFL and NFL merged in 1970.

League came close to setting a new scoring record

Through the end of Sunday afternoon's game with "Sunday Night Football" and "Monday Night Football" to go, the league was on pace to set a new record with an average of 50.1 points per game.

This is the highest scoring Week 1 since the 1970 NFL-AFL merger, though there are still two games to go pic.twitter.com/nrI0KsJvFw

— Ben Volin (@BenVolin) September 13, 2026

But the Giants and Cowboys combined for 48 in New York's Sunday night win, and the Chiefs and Broncos combined for a relatively paltry 41 on Monday. Blame the Broncos, whose offense was a disaster against an aggressive Kansas City defense.

Even with Denver's struggles, the Broncos and Chiefs needed just one point between them to set a new Week 1 NFL scoring record after Walker's touchdown early in the fourth quarter. A safety or field goal would have gotten the job done over the course of the game's final 14:39.

But Kansas City effectively milked the clock on offense and shackled Denver on defense to ensure that no more points were scored.

Regardless, it adds up to an explosive Week 1 of NFL action with multiple high-scoring affairs.

Bears lead the way under Ben Johnson

None were more notable than the barn-burner between the Chicago Bears and Carolina Panthers early Sunday in which Chicago secured a 59-37 win in Charlotte.

That matchup set the single-game scoring record for a Week 1 game when Chicago held a 52-37 lead with 4:00 remaining, and that was before the Bears piled on with another touchdown.

Why so many points?

So is this a sign of things to come this season? Have the NFL's rule changes over the years largely in the name of player safety made high-octane scoring affairs inevitable?

Former Steelers head coach and current NBC analyst Mike Tomlin offered a theory on "Sunday Night Football" suggesting that offenses have the early edge thanks to preseason and training camp regulations and practice habits.

"I think how we practice and how we prepare our teams today really kind of lends itself to offenses starting faster than they have historically," Tomlin said Sunday night "What I mean by that is there is less violence in team development. There are less padded practices. Even the drills that they do are more geared to skill development — 7 on 7 and things of that nature.

"Defenses spend less time shedding blocks and tackling than they used to 25 years ago when I came into the league."

Whether or not there's anything to that theory, one thing is clear. Defenses — including Denver's vaunted unit that repeatedly missed tackles Monday night — will have their work cut out for them as they prepare this week for Week 2.

item.title: Chris Olave looks ready to take another step after monster season opener
item.description: With the 2026 season opener in the books, let’s take at one of the stars of the game for New Orleans.
item.content:encoded:
New Orleans Saints wide receiver Chris Olave entered the 2026 season with plenty of expectations after earning second-team All-Pro honors last season.

After Sunday’s season opener against the Detroit Lions, it is difficult to imagine the Saints asking for much more from their star wideout.

Olave was one of the biggest reasons New Orleans was able to erase the 21-point deficit and nearly complete the incredible comeback, finishing with a career-high 182 receiving yards on 10 receptions. He was targeted 13 times and consistently gave Tyler Shough a reliable option as the Saints’ offense finally found its rhythm down the stretch.

For a Saints offense that struggled to get anything going early, Olave eventually became the spark it desperately needed.

The chemistry between him and Shough was especially encouraging, but it wasn’t surprising given what we’ve seen from the two this offseason.

Shough finished with a career-high 410 passing yards, and a large part of that production came from his willingness to continue looking Olave’s way when the Saints needed a big play. The two connected for several significant gains throughout the afternoon, including a 47-yard completion that helped New Orleans continue its comeback attempt.

Olave’s performance was also impressive considering the circumstances.

The Saints were shut out in the first half and eventually fell behind 21-0 before their offense finally came alive. Rather than disappearing when the game became difficult, Olave became increasingly important as New Orleans mounted its comeback.

The next step will be seeing whether Olave can stay healthy enough to turn this into a consistent season-long trend.

If Sunday was any indication, Olave could be in for a massive season.

Now, he will look to carry his momentum into Week 2’s matchup with the Baltimore Ravens.

item.title: The Day After the Day After: Houston Texans fall 36-31 to the Buffalo Bills
item.description: Yes! Football's back. No! Houston lost in a surprising barnburner. Let's review…'cause we like the pain?
item.content:encoded:
The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 1:

The Missed Turnovers: Last season, Houston ranked 3rd in forced turnovers. They left the game with zero. Yet, the stat sheet doesn’t always tell the tale. Houston missed at least three INTs and two fumble recoveries. Much has been said about Lassiter’s missed INT in the end zone. Jalen Pitre also had a golden opportunity to shut down a Bills’ drive with a near goal-line pick on a play that followed a Lassiter DPI giving the Bills the ball at the HOU 1. On a second quarter drive, Stingley somehow missed on a “[KITTEN] it” throw from Josh Allen to Dalton Kincaid. Later that drive, if Blankenship was a quarter of a second earlier in his jump, Houston gets that INT. In the fourth quarter, after Houston had taken a 31-30 lead, on the first play of the drive, Allen fumbled the snap, but he managed to jump on it. Then there was the first play of the next drive after Houston went three-and-out (More later). Turnovers can be a fickle mistress from year to year. To start this season, she betrayed the Texans. 

The Final Plays: For most of the game, the offense carried Houston. After a first drive fumble, Stroud regained his composure, and the offense line did their part to keep the game moving. Yet, on the second to last drive for the Texans, problems returned. While hindered by a curious (at best) play call for a second down toss sweep to the right, when the team had most of its success running to the offensive left, the line could not offer the push needed to get at least one 1st down. On the final drive, they got Houston to the BUF 9. However, G Ed Ingram got badly beaten, forcing a 9-yard sack. At 20 seconds, Houston was forced to either get to the end zone from the 18 or get out of bounds. The next pass was an incompletion, leaving Houston with maybe two more shots. Unfortunately, the right side of the line failed again, as T Trent Brown got beaten, allowing the strip-sack fumble of Stroud. While one could argue the final two sacks were not on him, Stroud can’t shake the turnover narrative. In the post-game comments, all the right things got said. Yet will the outside noise become reality for the line and Stroud?    

The Critical Play: 4th Quarter, 3:13, BUF ball, 1st and 10 @ BUF 4; RB James Cook rushes for 12 yards to the BUF 16, Derek Stingley Forced Fumble, recovered by BUF at the BUF 19

This game did not lack for game-altering plays. Yet, this missed fumble recovery looms large. Consider the opening play of that final Bills’ drive. After Kroeger and the coverage units pinned the Bills at the 4, Buffalo went with a run play. Cook busted through the Texans defense to get out past the 16-yard line. Then comes Stingley, who knocks the ball out of Cook’s right arm with a well-timed punch. Should Houston recover there, they would have the ball inside the Bills’ 20. Worst case, the Bills use all of their TOs, Houston kicks the FG to go up 34-30, and the Bills, with only the possible 2-minute warning, have to go to the end zone with no timeouts. Possibly the Bills still get the TD, but the percentages would favor Houston a bit more, and perhaps with the momentum of forcing a turnover and punt in the previous two possessions, that might have been enough. 

FUN WITH NUMBERS: 

8/76: Average number of penalties/average penalty yards for Texans in season-openers under Ryans: The first game of the season tends to be a bit sloppy, and the refs got plenty of arm exercises in this one. 7 flags for a whooping 106 yards for the Texans, 10 penalties for 85 yards against the Bills. For Houston, 61 of those yards came on two back-breaking flags (46-yard DPI on Lassiter setting up a Bills TD and a 15-yard Roughing the Passer on Mario Edwards keeping another Bills drive alive). In the three season-opening losses, the Texans average 9 flags for 91 yards. At this point, it is a feature of the Ryans regime that flags will be an issue to start off the season.  

GAME BALLS: 

RB David Montgomery: 20 carries for 60 yards and 3 receptions for 19 yards might not seem like much, but throw in 2 rushing TDs, along with a receiving TD, and he showed that Houston might have the back they need. It also allowed Woody Marks to be that change-up back, a role that will suit him better (9 rushes for 42 yards). It wasn’t enough in this game, but especially later in the season, getting nearly 30 total rushes at nearly 4 yards a clip with the RBs will be a good thing. 

P Kai Kroeger and the Houston Punt Coverage Units: Kroeger had 4 punts, averaging 52.0 yards/kick and landing two inside the 5. The coverage units limited the Bills to two returns for 10 total yards. Those two punts had the perfect height/spin to allow the coverage units to get down the field and pin the Bills deep in their territory. In theory, a great set up for that Texans’ defense. In reality…not so much.

TE Dalton Kincaid: Yes, an opposing player is on the list. Then again, he fried any Texans’ defender he came against, from All-Pro Stingley to Blakenship. Coming back after being injured the past two seasons, against what may still be among the best secondaries in the league, and leaving with 5 receptions for 130 yards, including two 35+ yard receptions…yeah, give him credit for that one.   

SHOULD BE FORCED TO WRITE A DOCTORAL DISSERATION ON HOUSTON’S COVERAGE SCHEMES WHILE LISTENING TO MATTHEW MCCONAUGHEY, TED CRUZ AND CAL MCNAIR ATTEMPT TO SING OPERA-STYLE “THE EYES OF TEXAS”

S Reed Blankenship: That gamble on the INT backfired spectacularly, as DJ Moore got one of the easiest TD’s he’ll ever have. He didn’t exactly the best day in coverage against the Bills receivers, including getting torched by TE Dalton Kincaid on the final drive. His stats (7 total tackles (4 solo)) are the definition of empty. Arguably, the entire secondary could reside here, but Blankenship leads the pack.

DC Matt Burke: The Most Interesting Defensive Coordinator in the World…did not have a good game at all. Sure, Josh Allen can make many a good defense look mortal, but Burke did not seem to have the right answers for slowing down the Bills’ offense. Perhaps most damning, he did not think to have a spy on Allen on a play that resulted in a 21-yard TD run when no defender touched the QB known for rushing. The second half went a bit better, but even those adjustments weren’t enough. Burke usually calls great defense since he took over the defensive play-calling. Not this day. 

NFL/TV Network Executives: The game of the weekend, and it was relegated to Sunday early afternoon? Sure, there are lots of factors to consider with primetime and marquee matchup times. It got national attention at its timeslot, but this seemed like a real marquee matchup, and one that did live up to the hype that a national/stand-alone game should promise. 

The Ohio State 4th Quarter Game Plan: Think Houston had a bad 4th Quarter? They didn’t have the worst one in the state of Texas this past weekend. That distinction must go to the Buckeyes of Ohio State. Up 23-3 in the 4th, they proceeded to get out scored 21-0 to end the game. If you are a Longhorn fan (or really can’t stand Ohio State), congratulations, you may continue your crowing. If not, well, I don’t think the insufferability of the previously mentioned groups will go away anytime soon.    

For the 3rd time in 4 seasons under DeMeco Ryans, the Texans start 0-1. Every time they started 0-1, they at least started 0-2. They will look to avoid that fate when they host the Cincinnati Bengals back at Reliant Stadium for 12:00 CDT kickoff.

item.title: The Chiefs finally found the explosive run game they’ve been missing
item.description: Kenneth Walker III gives Chiefs another dangerous element
item.content:encoded:
During the 2024 NFL season, the Kansas City Chiefs generated seven explosive runs on offense, defined as runs of 20 yards or more. That was near the bottom of the league. A year ago the Chiefs offense managed only three of those such plays — the worst mark in the NFL — with just one such run coming from a running back.

On Monday night against the Denver Broncos, new Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III had two such runs alone, doubling the number of explosive runs from a running back from last season, and giving this Kansas City offense a dangerous new component.

By the time the game ended, Walker had picked up 173 rushing yards on 23 carries, with those rushing yards representing a career-high number. Those were also the most rushing yards for a Chiefs player in their Kansas City debut, besting the 148 rushing yards from Kareem Hunt back in 2017.

It was also the fourth-highest rushing total from a player in their first game with a new team in league history.

Andy Reid did not waste any time getting Walker involved in the offense, as the new Chiefs running back had seven carries for 32 yards on Kansas City’s first drive of the 2026 season. Those seven plays includes runs on the interior:

And plays to the edge:

There was something else notable about those two runs: They came with Mahomes aligned under center, rather than in the shotgun. In fact, four of Walker’s carries on the opening drive came with Mahomes under center, a sign that Kansas City was hoping to improve another weakness of their running game from the past few seasons.

By the time the night came to a close, the vast majority of Walker’s rushing yards came from the under-center run game:

That included both of those explosive running plays. The first came with just over four minutes left in the first half, with the game knotted at 7-7. Walker picks up 28 yards on a run to the left side, behind a zone-blocking scheme and out of 12 offensive personnel, with tight ends Travis Kelce and Noah Gray in the game:

As noted, watch left guard Kingsley Suamataia get to the second level on his block, helping to clear the way for Walker.

Then came the big play, a 60-yard touchdown run on 4th-and-inches early in the second half.:

Kansas City used heavy personnel on this play, not only bringing a pair of extra linemen into the game but also defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga, who lined up at fullback.

The result? A 60-yard scoring burst that saw Walker break not only a tackle near the line of scrimmage, but another tackle more than 40 yards downfield, as he bullied his way into the end zone.

Missed tackles were another theme from last night, as Walker forced 14 missed tackles against the Broncos, the most by a Kansas City player since 2018:

The story coming into the game was the health of Mahomes, who was playing nine months to the day after tearing the ACL and LCL in his left knee. Mahomes did look rusty at times, but a touchdown scamper to close off Kansas City’s opening drive likely sent shivers down the spines of AFC defensive coordinators.

But what we saw from this Chiefs running game, and Walker, might be even scarier.

item.title: Chiefs' first-round rookie CB Mansoor Delane intercepts Bo Nix in his first NFL series, then ruled out with shoulder injury
item.description: Delane immediately paid off on Kansas City's steep investment to acquire him, then left the field with injury concerns.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs raised eyebrows when they traded up to the No. 6 pick in April's NFL Draft to select LSU cornerback Mansoor Delane.

One series into the season, he made an immediate impact before leaving the game with an injury.

The Chiefs sacked the Denver Broncos' Bo Nix on the first play of their season opener on Monday night. On the third play, Nix threw a downfield pass into double coverage on third-and-11.

Delane was there to make a play and intercepted Nix near midfield.

The interception set Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes up for his first game action since sustaining a torn ACL last season.

The Chiefs pounded the ground game, and Mahomes capped a 10-play, 46-yard drive with a 15-yard touchdown scramble through the middle of Denver's defense. The Chiefs rolled to a 31-10 win.

It added up to a sensational start to Kansas City's season but one that come at a cost.

Delane wasn't on the field for Kansas City's second defensive series, and the Chiefs announced that he was questionable to return with a shoulder injury. They ruled him out for the game at the start of the third quarter.

The nature and severity of his injury was not initially clear, and head coach Andy Reid said after the game "we're just gonna see where that goes from here" when asked about the injury.

Delane will reportedly undergo an MRI on Tuesday, per NFL Network. He did have X-rays on his shoulder, which came back negative.

Chiefs made steep investment to acquire Delane

The Chiefs were in dire need of secondary help after trading All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie to the Los Angeles Rams. Their answer to fill that void was drafting Delane, and they were willing to pay to acquire him.

In order to get Delane at No. 6, the Chiefs traded the No. 9, No. 74 (third round) and No. 148 picks (fifth round) to the Cleveland Browns, a price that some critics considered too steep for a cornerback.

Delane came from LSU with an All-American pedigree and filled a need, and the price was right for a Chiefs team seeking to continue to capitalize on Mahomes' prime.

He rewarded that confidence by joining a short list of players to record an interception on their first NFL drive.
