item.title: Chiefs CB Mansoor Delane to have MRI on shoulder
item.description: Chiefs first-round pick Mansoor Delane had a brief, but eventful NFL debut on Monday night.
item.content:encoded:
Chiefs first-round pick Mansoor Delane had a brief, but eventful NFL debut on Monday night.

Delane recorded his first interception as a pro when he snagged a pass from Broncos quarterback Bo Nix on the third play of the game. That would be the last contribution of the night for the rookie cornerback, however.

Delane went to the locker room with a shoulder injury during the Broncos' second offensive possession. Head coach Andy Reid did not have an update on his condition after the game and Mike Garafolo of NFL Media reports that he will have an MRI on Tuesday.

Garafolo adds that X-rays were negative and that there is hope that Delane, who also dealt with a shoulder injury in the spring, emerged with a sprain. Tuesday's test should provide a better picture of how long it will be before he's back in the Kansas City secondary.

item.title: NFL Week 1 makes odd history with every game ending by a different final margin
item.description: Kansas City’s 21-point win over Denver made some NFL history
item.content:encoded:
Monday night’s game between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Denver Broncos made a bit of NFL history.

It marked the first time a 16-game slate where every game was won by a different number of points.

Working our way through the schedule, you can see how this came together. Entering Monday night, games were won by the following scores:

1: Detroit Lions 31, New Orleans Saints 30
2: Philadelphia Eagles 24, Washington Commanders 22
3: Seattle Seahawks 13, New England Patriots 10
5: Buffalo Bills 36, Houston Texans 31
6: Cincinnati Bengals 33, Tampa Bay Buccaneers 27
7: Pittsburgh Steelers 20, Atlanta Falcons 13
8: New York Giants 28, Dallas Cowboys 20
12: Arizona Cardinals 26, Los Angeles Chargers 14
13: New York Jets 23, Tennessee Titans 10
14: Las Vegas Raiders 27, Miami Dolphins 13
17: Minnesota Vikings 39, Green Bay Packers 22
18: Baltimore Ravens 41, Indianapolis Colts 23
20: San Francisco 49ers 27, Los Angeles Rams 7
22: Chicago Bears 59, Carolina Panthers 37
24: Jacksonville Jaguars 34, Cleveland Browns 10

This was pointed out on social media by various accounts, including NFL analyst Lee Sharpe:

That meant that the 2026 Week 1 slate had already tied the Week 7 slate from last season, which saw 15 different scoring margins, for the most in NFL history.

Then the Chiefs, in the return of Patrick Mahomes, defeated the Broncos by a final score of 31-10, for a 21-point margin.

Meaning all 16 games were won by a different margin of points, for the first time in league history.

Welcome to the history books, Week 1.

item.title: Lions vs. Saints Song of the Game: ‘Paradise by the dashboard light’ by Meat Loaf
item.description: Meat Loaf’s ballad about a young, passionately-crazed couple perfectly encaptures Lions vs. Saints.
item.content:encoded:
The rush to judgment in the NFL after Week 1 is maddening. We enter the season fully aware that September football is ugly, and Week 1 lies. Yet the dizzying speed, emotion, and overall cacophony of the NFL’s return creates monsters of us all.

FIRE THIS GUY! THAT QUARTERBACK SUCKS! I TOLD YOU THEY WERE GOING TO BE TERRIBLE THIS YEAR!

The Detroit Lions eked out a win over the New Orleans Saints, and no matter what your expectations for the team were in 2026, this game confirmed those greatest fears and/or highest expectations. The first half proves the Lions, when firing on all cylinders, are capable of blowing out anyone. Or the second half definitively shows Kelvin Sheppard is a fraud, the secondary stinks, and the Lions’ Super Bowl window is closed.

Y’all, can we just sleep on it?

Detroit Lions Week 1 Song of the Game: “Paradise By The Dashboard Light” by Meat Loaf

Yes, “Song of the Game” is back due to popular demand me just wanting to do it again and bring some fun back to the site. If you weren’t around or don’t remember, Song of the Game is exactly what it sounds like: a song that attempts to capture the essence of the Lions’ game. We talk about it here, do it weekly, and then we have a crazy, disjointed playlist by the end of the season.

If you want to relive previous Lions seasons, you can find the playlists we curated below: 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022. And if you want to read previous versions of our Song of the Game columns, you can find those here.

It’s only appropriate that the first song to kick off this playlist is one that matches the Lions’ season opener in length. Meat Loaf’s most iconic duet stretches nearly eight-and-a-half minutes, taking the listener through a journey of love, thrills, painful indecisiveness, and regret. Yeah, that sounds about right.

Now, I’m going to admit right here that this song is overtly sexual, and it’s going to make for some awkward metaphors. So buckle up. This one isn’t for the faint of hearts.

We’re glowing like the metal on the edge of a knife
Glowing like the metal on the edge of a knife

The Lions’ 2026 season got off to a somewhat strong start. After shaking off a three-and-out, the offense put together an impressive 13-play, 89-yard drive. Jahmyr Gibbs had gains of 11, 21, and 11 yards before eventually walking in untouched for the season’s first score. The rushing lanes were occasionally gaping, the blocking schemes were complicated, and the offensive line—despite losing Christian Mahogany halfway through the drive—was humming. Oh, baby, we were cookin’.

After Meat Loaf and Ellen Foley spend the first 3:30 glam rocking to each other about the sex their characters are about to have, the song kicks in a funky beat and a faux radio call of a baseball game is laid over the track. It’s about as blatant a sex metaphor as you can get, as the not-so-convincing radio announcer describes a series of plays in which the runner crosses each base and nears home.

He’s taking a pretty big lead out there
Almost daring him to try and pick him off

The Lions were inching closer and closer to a decisive Week 1 win. Derrick Barnes, interception. Gibbs, touchdown. Roger McCreary, sack fumble. Amon-Ra St. Brown, touchdown.

Ford Field was feeling it, Lions fans were in awe of the team’s defense finally coming together with a marriage of pass rush and coverage. It was starting to feel like Detroit’s offseason plan was coming together perfectly.

Stop right there

Just before we find out whether this “base runner” is “safe at home,” Foley screams out to stop everything. The song comes to a screeching halt. Before the baseball player is ready to “consummate” his trip around the bases, she begs for long-term commitment and faith.

And just like the Lions failed to seal the deal cleanly, Meat Loaf struggled to find an answer.

I gotta know right now, before we go any further
Do you love me? Will you love me forever?

Baby, baby, let me sleep on it
Well, let me sleep on it
I’ll give you an answer in the morning

As with every NFL fanbase after every game, the noise following the Lions’ 31-30 win has been loud and exaggerated. The doubters now have definitive proof the Lions are doomed. The endlessly faithful point to the first half as irrefutable evidence everything is going to be fine once things settle in.

Me, I’m not so sure. I’m not ready to give an answer. There were promising developments in the run game, offensive line, and pass rush. But there were troubling, ominous signs in the secondary, defensive game plan, and offensive inconsistency.

Everyone is in a rush to find out answers and come to undeniable conclusions. Why can’t anyone just admit: we still don’t know. We need more time. Let’s sleep on it.

Meat Loaf’s marathon of a song ends in tragedy. The male character expresses grief, regret, and sorrow for those exciting days. He’s stuck in a relationship bonded by carnal pleasure instead of true love. He’s tormented by his past, hasty choices and just wants it all to end.

Unlike the narrator, though, the Lions have a chance to quickly put the past behind them. Thursday is a new opportunity to recapture that glowing edge of a knife and find true success—not just fleeting sparks.

item.title: Chiefs News: Travis Kelce moves into 2nd place for all-time TEs list
item.description: The latest Chiefs news, brought fresh to you every morning!
item.content:encoded:
Amid the Kansas City Chiefs’ 31-10 blowout of the Denver Broncos in Week 1, tight end Travis Kelce etched his name further into the stone of NFL history.

He didn’t set any speed records on the big catch-and-run Kelce had in the second half, but he did inch closer to legendary Chiefs tight end Tony Gonzalez on the all-time tight end receiving list.

The latest Kansas City Chiefs news

Chiefs’ Travis Kelce moves into second place for all-time tight end receiving yards | NFL.com

Predictably, Kelce downplayed the individual milestone when speaking to ESPN’s Laura Rutledge after the game. 

“It’s a good feeling to get this win, all the other stuff is just hoopla now,” he said. 

Kelce caught a 59-yard pass from old friend Patrick Mahomes in the third quarter to put him past longtime Dallas Cowboys stalwart Jason Witten for second all-time. Ahead of Monday’s season opener, Kelce had 13,002 yards, needing 45 to surpass Witten (13,046).

The catch was a turn-back-the-clock moment for Kelce, standing as his longest reception since Week 15, 2021, when he turned in a 69-yarder versus the Los Angeles Chargers. 

Patrick Mahomes Gets Win In Return: 3 Takeaways As Chiefs Beat Broncos | FOX Sports

Chiefs Look Like Contenders In Mahomes’ Return

There was punctuation as well – Mahomes found rookie running back Emmett Johnson for 25 yards on a third down, setting up a flip-toss touchdown to Walker for a 31-10 lead to put the game out of reach. Mahomes improved to 8-0 at home against Denver in his career, one of the longest home streaks for any quarterback against any opponent. After his shaky start, Mahomes went 11-for-13 for 145 yards and two touchdowns to pull away.

Kenneth Walker III, Patrick Mahomes lead Chiefs’ win vs. Broncos | ESPN

Mahomes’ toughness and athleticism were on display on his 10th snap, as he scrambled out of the pocket and dove — while being hit by two defenders — for a 15-yard touchdown. His top speed during that scramble reached 15.8 mph, which was 2.5 mph faster than his average speed on rushing attempts last season, according to Next Gen Stats.

“Going for the end zone, it kind of gave me that confidence that I can go out there and be myself,” said Mahomes, who underwent surgery in December to repair a torn ACL and LCL in his left knee. “I just wanted to play. I had done so much rehab and so much work to put myself in this position. I just wanted to get out there and play. This is what you do it for.

“That was definitely the moment, physically, to say all this work has paid off. I didn’t feel anything.”

From front to back, Chiefs’ defense brought the heat against the Denver Broncos | The Kansas City Star

The Broncos finished with 176 total yards and nine first downs. They rushed for 61 and went 2 of 12 on third-down conversions.

“Our third down numbers weren’t good, our rushing numbers weren’t good, pick your spots,” Broncos head coach Sean Payton said.

Chiefs cornerback L’Jarius Sneed, who returned to Kansas City after spending the previous two seasons with the Tennessee Titans, said Monday’s performance should end any doubt about this defense’s capability.

“We come into a new season trying to figure out where we’re at, and we come out and play like this,” Sneed said. “This should build great confidence.”

Kansas City Chiefs manage to deliver rushing performance at Arrowhead Stadium not seen in 10 years | Yahoo! Sports

This rushing performance also made a bit of history for the Chiefs, as it marked the first time in 10 years that they had rushed for 220 yards at Arrowhead Stadium.

Ironically, their last 200-yard+ rushing performance at home came against the Denver Broncos as well, as the team rushed for 238 yards on Christmas Day 2016.

What makes this stat even more prevalent is that both games resulted in the Chiefs picking up wins with almost identical scorelines.

The Chiefs’ 2026 opener saw them beat the Broncos 31-10, while their Christmas Day outing in 2016 saw them defeat the Broncos 33-10.

Kansas City Chiefs HC Andy Reid proves he still has his fastball after dusting off a play from the 1930s for RB Kenneth Walker | A to Z Sports

Week 1 against Denver, the Chiefs pulled out a play from even earlier. This time it was a 1936 play the team watched on grainy black-and-white film and mastered throughout training camp. The play, dubbed “Heisman,” resulted in a 2-yard touchdown reception for RB Kenneth Walker. It included QB Justin Fields, QB Patrick Mahomes, and TE Travis Kelce aligned in the backfield in a one-point stance.

Kansas City, of course, has run other trick plays over the years. You’ll remember “Corn Dog”, “Snow Globe”, “Bloated Tebow Pass“, and “Hungry Pig Right.” All of these plays were hallmarks of Reid’s tenure with the Chiefs, and those moments captured what it was like to have fun playing football in Kansas City. He brought that back again with this latest iteration in Week 1’s 30-10 win.

Around the NFL

This Eagles offensive lineman admits he was ‘a complete liability’ and needed to be shut down | The Athletic

Dickerson confirmed while speaking on his Monday night radio show on 94.1 WIP that the Eagles had informed him of their plan to place him on injured reserve. “I was a complete liability yesterday,” Dickerson said. “I know I said earlier in camp, I shouldn’t be out there until I feel healthy.”

The Eagles lineman said he has bone bruising in his right knee and was told it would not heal if he kept “banging it up,” and that he needed to shut it down. Dickerson said the injury occurred when he “got rolled up on in practice” a few weeks ago. He had hoped that the injury would improve. He underwent imaging on Monday, when it was determined that time off would be the “best plan going forward.”

Sources: Drew Brees mulled playing for Broncos in AFC title game | ESPN

After the Denver Broncos lost starting quarterback Bo Nix to a fractured ankle in their overtime playoff victory against the Buffalo Bills, Denver’s then-offensive coordinator Joe Lombardi and offensive assistant Pete Carmichael had discussions with Brees about the former star quarterback coming out of retirement to be ready for the AFC Championship Game, sources told ESPN.

Brees had turned 47 years old just two days before Nix sustained the ankle injury Jan. 17. Brees spoke to Lombardi and Carmichael, his longtime assistant coaches with the New Orleans Saints, early in the week ahead of Denver’s AFC Championship Game showdown against the New England Patriots, telling them that he wanted to first work out to see how his body would respond.

In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride

3 takeaways from the Chiefs’ season-opening beatdown of the Broncos

The pass game will open up

It took a while for the Chiefs’ offense to get over 15 passing yards. It was almost comical how much of the offense’s output was on Walker’s shoulders for much of the game. In the first half, Mahomes had just two completions over 12 pass attempts; neither catch resulted in a first down.

In the second half, Mahomes was much more efficient. He completed 13 of 15 passes; eight of those catches resulted in a first down or a touchdown.

item.title: Miami Dolphins’ Most Valuable Player | Week One | Radiant Rookie
item.description: Caleb Douglas nabs five passes for 94 yards in NFL debut.
item.content:encoded:
Don’t you dare think I can’t see you rolling your eyes at your screen right now…

Yes, despite the fact that the Miami Dolphins lost to the Las Vegas Raiders by a score of 27-13 on Sunday, marking a disappointing debut for new head coach Jeff Hafley, we will be naming a Most Valuable ‘Phin for that contest. And yes, despite the fact that the 2026 season has the potential to be one of the most frustrating years of Dolphins football in recent memory, we will be picking an MVP each and every week this season.

If that bothers you, don’t click. It’s really that simple.

However, for those who are viewing the 2026 season through the right lens, we will be finding silver linings and highlighting players who are impressing despite the organization’s current struggles in an effort to put some attention on the positives this year — however few of those may exist.

Miami Dolphins Week One MVP – WR Caleb Douglas

In his professional debut, Douglas had an historic performance — nabbing five balls for 94 yards. His receiving yards total was the most for any Dolphins rookie receiver in his first NFL game, but was also tied with Tyreek Hill (2022) for the most receiving yards for any receiver in their first game with the team in the franchise’s history.

For a player who many thought was overdrafted when he was selected by new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan in the third round of the 2026 NFL Draft, Douglas’ debut was a delightful one to witness for Dolphins fans.

Let’s hope that he can continue to progress forward as the season rolls on, and his counterpart, Chris Bell, can begin to contribute in meaningful ways as well. Quarterback Malik Willis and the organization as a whole would be significantly better for it.

MVP TRACKER

Week One – WR Caleb Douglas

item.content:encoded:
Football is in full swing now, but somehow the fall weather is lagging behind, by a lot. The college football season just wrapped up its official week two and the NFL is now fully underway after wrapping up a high scoring week one.

A few weeks ago we ran through the league to see where our former Rebs ended up after NFL cut day, now it’s time to check in and see how they fared in week one.

Evan Engram paced the Denver Broncos in receiving with 43 yards and a touchdown on four receptions against the Kansas City Chiefs on Monday Night Football.

DK Metcalf also hauled in four catches for 40 yards on a team high 10 targets in the Steelers’ victory over Atlanta.

Tavious Robinson was a force for the Baltimore Ravens’ defense, finishing with three tackles, a sack and four QB hits. In the same game, Tahj Chambers registered his first NFL tackle for the Colts.

Princely Umanmielen had three tackles and a sack for the Carolina Panthers in their loss to Chicago.

After being cut by the Dallas Cowboys, Sam Williams signed with the Cleveland Browns. He had an immediate impact, finishing with four tackles on the game.

Tre Harris finished the game with three catches on six targets for just 20 yards.

Jaxson Dart was easily the Rebel of the week after a masterclass against the Dallas Cowboys. In his first opening game as the starter, Dart finished 23 for 29 passing for 230 yards and three touchdowns. He added 54 yards on the ground rushing while not turning the ball over once.

AJ Brown suited up for his new squad, but was injured early with a high ankle sprain. The New England Patriots have since placed him on the IR. De’Zhaun Stribling is also expected to miss his first month of action with an ankle injury of his own. Despite that injury and the absence of Brandon Aiyuk and Ricky Pearsall, Jordan Watkins was a healthy scratch and inactive for the 49ers.

item.title: Panthers vs Bears Game Review: Hasty generalizations
item.description: It was bad, but somehow still a big improvement.
item.content:encoded:
The full story of an NFL season is not written after a single game. Even one where you are force fed a 50-burger in your own stadium. It was a hard one to stomach for anyone rooting for the Carolina Panthers, but despite a lopsided final score and number of concerning takeaways, it’s probably the best start to a season in the last 5 years.

If I had to sum up the reason why, it’s that even when things looked bad, they still looked competitive. We are all mindful that that is a shamefully low bar, but the point remains that it’s a vast improvement over what has been the recent quality of football coming out of Charlotte, North Carolina.

So, let us all not jump to the conclusions that we may want to after a single week. Even if this one week stirs up some still unresolved trauma from the 2024 Panthers defense that allowed almost 32 points per game. Let us look on the bright side and decide that even if the Panthers defense is that bad, scoring 37 points a game means the Panthers will still win an average football game.

Feel better yet?

No? Then in the spirit of overreacting to Week 1, let’s make some hasty generalizations based on what we saw on Sunday afternoon.

Jalen Coker will be the best Panthers receiver of all time

A receiver putting up 8 receptions for 138 yards and 2 touchdowns a game? That’s 136 catches for 2,346 yards and 34 touchdowns in a whole season. Make room Steve Smith, there’s another triple-crown winner coming through. He doesn’t even need separation to make it happen, either. According to NFL’s NextGenStats, Coker only had an average 1.9 yards of separation at the time of catch or incompletion – 8th worst total in the league.

The Offensive Line is the most consistent in the entire NFL

If you thought that both tackles being out for Week 1 and starting a new budget free agent acquisition at center was going to be a problem, you were wrong. In fact, the Panthers offense line looked about as good as it possibly could have given the circumstances as no starter had a run blocking or pass blocking grade considered below average. Hats off to the winners of PFF’s Offensive Line of the Week.

Give Bryce Young all of the money

If Baker Mayfield is going to sign for 3 years, $165 million to only put up 217 yards and 0 touchdowns, surely Bryce Young’s 361 passing yards and 4 total touchdowns must be worth $60 million a year? Young is currently 3rd in the NFL in passing yards, tied for 2nd in passing touchdowns and top 10 in a bevy of other important stats including EPA/Play (9th – +0.27), completion % over expected (9th – 6.6%), yards per attempt (4th – 9.3) and average depth of target (10th – 9.8 yards).

Strip Derrick Brown of his captaincy

The Bears scored 8 touchdowns, but 2 of them came on the back of some rough decisions from one of the purported team stalwarts. Mistake number one was leveling Caleb William’s on cheap shot that was flagged for unnecessary roughness after a throwaway that ultimately turned a 3rd and 20 into 1st and goal. I can almost forgive that one as William’s must have been immensely frustrating to deal with the entire afternoon. Williams had nearly a 20% completion percentage over expected and had 10 scrambles for 65 yards and 2 rushing touchdowns. Every time they though they had him, he pulled a Houdini act to get away.

But you know what is unforgivable?

Taking away a big man interception because you lined up offsides. Do you know how rare it is for a 332 lb defensive lineman to intercept a football? Neither do I, but I know it’s not often, much less from the literal 1 yard line. A big man shows soft hands and a hero’s heart to pluck a ball right out of the air in the Panther’s time of most dire need – and it’s called back because your helmet was over the line? Derrick Brown deserves a lot of love for what he has done for the Panthers, but this is an outrage that cannot be tolerated.

It’s not all over yet and there is still plenty of road ahead on this journey. We’ll see you next week after the Panthers take on the Atlanta Falcons. Until then, Keep Pounding

item.title: NFL Power Rankings Week 2: Not Overreacting To Kickoff Weekend
item.description: Week 1 is in the books, and we’ll do our best not to overreact to another season-opening weekend full of action with @AaronLemingNFL’s power rankings!
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 NFL regular season is underway, and with that, Week 1 is in the books. As usual, the opening week of football has proven to be one of the most unpredictable in the football calendar. Unlike previous seasons, the opener kicked off on a Wednesday, followed by the NFL’s first game in Australia. While it’s great to have football back, it’s always important not to overreact too much to the results from the weekend. With that in mind, let’s dive into our WCG Week 2 NFL Power Rankings as we turn the page on the season opener. 

1. Seattle Seahawks (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Thank God Sam Darnold’s Injury Is Short-Term. Pulling out a 13-10 victory is one thing, but without the long-term health of Darnold secured, their season looks much different moving forward. The good news is that while there’s no definitive diagnosis for the Seahawks’ quarterback quite yet, the consensus is that he avoided anything long-term or season-ending. Assuming this doesn’t end in an IR stint, Seattle will be just fine, and the best is yet to come.

2. Buffalo Bills (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: D.J. Moore is going to make a big difference for Josh Allen. That might be enough to get their offense back to a Super Bowl level. The bigger focus will be on the defense. Despite their win, they still gave up 31 points. The talent is there; it might just take some time with a new coaching staff to get things firing correctly. 

3. Baltimore Ravens (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: The reports of Lamar Jackson’s demise were premature. He’s back. The bigger question is whether their defense can return to form under head coach Jesse Minter. This is a highly talented team that underachieved last year, but they must get a better return on investment from some of their higher-paid players if they hope to return to Super Bowl contention this season. 

4. San Francisco 49ers (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: If Thursday night was any indication, a healthy defense could make a world of difference this season. The 49ers looked dangerous, fast, and well-rounded on both sides of the football. Barring better health than previous seasons, San Francisco could contend for the NFC West title this season. 

5. Los Angeles Rams (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: With Myles Garrett on IR for four-to-six weeks, how quickly Aaron Donald can get into shape might dictate whether or not they can hang in the division race once Garrett returns. The Rams might have to rely on other veterans like Matthew Stafford, Davante Adams, and Puka Nukua to keep this team on track while they wait for their defense to take shape. 

6. Jacksonville Jaguars (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Browns or not, quarterback Trevor Lawrence’s growth under head coach Liam Coen does not appear to be a half-season fluke. Even more impressive is the defense’s continued improvement. Despite Deshaun Watson’s overall numbers, the game was well out of hand before the Browns offense did anything of note. This is a well-rounded team with a potential Top 5-7 quarterback reaching his peak. 

7. Chicago Bears (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: The offense’s Year 2 jump under Ben Johnson is evident, but the defense might keep them from being a legitimate Super Bowl contender. The Bears must find some defensive balance, and it must happen in a hurry. Better health will help, but for now, the offense will face continued pressure to produce 30-plus points per game. 

8. Kansas City Chiefs

Initial Week 1 Thought: Are the Chiefs back or were they ever gone? The defense looked great, but plenty of questions remain on offense, including how to get their pass catchers open. With that in mind, Kenneth Walker III sure looked good in his Kansas City debut. 

9. Denver Broncos (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: The Broncos’ blowout loss on the road in Kansas City felt like a prime example of a game that nobody should overreact to. That said, that was about as bad as Denver has looked in a few years, so hopefully it was a fluke rather than the regression some have been expecting in 2026. 

10. Houston Texans (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Houston’s early-season struggles continue into another year, but C.J. Stroud’s 274-yard passing performance was promising after how the playoffs ended. Assuming the defense can get back on track, they should have more than enough talent on both sides of the ball to compete with Jacksonville for another AFC South title. 

11. New England Patriots (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: This year’s top regression candidate will have to contend with a (0-1) start and one of the league’s toughest schedules. Even so, don’t bail on the Patriots quite yet. There’s plenty of talent on both sides of the ball, and it’s hard to imagine that Drake Maye will experience the same struggles he did on Wednesday night in Seattle. 

12. Detroit Lions (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Even if it shows 31 points in the box score, there’s going to be some patience needed with Drew Petzing taking over the play calling. Part of that comes from blowing a 21-point lead, but Jahmyr Gibbs was the only offensive player with typical production against a Saints team still trying to find its footing. We’ll see how they look on a short week in Buffalo. 

13. Cincinnati Bengals (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: With four sacks and four takeaways, over time the Bengals may finally prove to have a Super Bowl-caliber defense. Now, it’s time to get Ja’Marr Chase and their highly paid receivers going in the passing game. Regardless, there’s plenty to be excited about in Cincinnati. 

14. Philadelphia Eagles (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Despite scoring 24 points, the Eagles’ lack of killer instinct on offense should still concern folks, even after bringing in yet another offensive coordinator. Saquon Barkley looked better than he did for most of last season, but has still yet to show the same burst. The same could be said for quarterback Jalen Hurts and the passing attack as a whole. 

15. Green Bay Packers (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: The organization put its faith in head coach Matt LaFleur with an extension, but their inability to finish games is becoming a very concerning trend that cannot be ignored. In fact, the Packers have four losses that all had 90% or better win probabilities heading into the fourth quarter. Now they must figure out whether they are the league’s unluckiest team or have a systemic issue that needs to be addressed.

16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Without overreacting, it’s fair to say that the Chargers’ Week 1 offensive output was highly disappointing. That’s the key to them getting back to the playoffs and finding some success this season. It’s fair to expect things to improve, but it was also fair to expect a much better product in their first game. We’ll see how Jim Harbaugh plans to get his team to respond. 

17. Minnesota Vikings (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: How serious is Kyler Murray’s concussion? Their season-long success might rely on it. In the short-term, they pulled off an impressive victory against the Packers and have a chance to get to 2-0, with both wins coming in the division if they can take care of business on Sunday in Chicago. We’ll see if Kevin O’Connell sticks with Carson Wentz or decides to give J.J. McCarthy a spot start while waiting on Murray to clear concussion protocol. 

18. Pittsburgh Steelers (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: The defense still has some juice, but how concerned should we be that they couldn’t handle the lowly Falcons on their third quarterback more convincingly? A lot of that comes down to an underwhelming offense, led by a well over-the-hill Aaron Rodgers. This roster has an older core, and it’s fair to wonder what their ceiling is moving forward. 

19. New York Giants (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Game 1 of John Harbaugh was extremely impressive. If Jaxson Dart is a plus-starter, they could turn this thing around quickly, especially with a defense loaded with talent, particularly on the defensive line. The future looks much brighter than it did nine months ago, and there’s little reason to doubt their viability for a playoff stretch if they continue to play as they did on Sunday night. 

20. Dallas Cowboys (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Either the defense is going to require some patience through growing pains or this group isn’t nearly as improved as originally believed. We’ll see if this was a Week 1 bump in the road or we simply overrated their improvements because of how much reach Jerry Jones has in the media. The next few games should give us a true idea of where they stand.

21. Carolina Panthers (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Bryce Young is clearly making strides, and they have plenty of weapons on the offensive side of the ball, but giving up 59 points at home (at any point in the season) is a serious red flag. Luckily, they are in the NFC South. Will that be enough to get back to the playoffs? I’m not convinced without tangible defensive improvements soon.

22. Indianapolis Colts (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Daniel Jones’ string of underwhelming starts continued into this season, but even more concerning is a defense that gave up 41 points and 500-plus yards to the Ravens. The Colts are used to slow starts, but some concerning trends need to be fixed quickly. 

23. New Orleans Saints (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Even in defeat, there was plenty to like about Tyler Shough and the entire Saints’ second-half performance in Detroit. The NFC South is very winnable, and they should be right there until the end. Patience might be required though, so buckle up. 

24. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: The concern with extending Baker Mayfield to big money was ceiling. After three fumbles lost on Sunday, those concerns only amplify. What is the overall ceiling for this team? Even in the worst division in football, there’s no guarantee that they can get back to the playoffs. If they do, how viable a threat are they? 

25. Washington Commanders (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: It felt like the Commanders were never truly in their two-point loss to the Eagles, but more importantly, how sustainable is David Blough’s offense if it takes three quarters for Jayden Daniels to surpass 100 yards? The defense looked much improved, but the offense raises serious questions, especially about how quickly they abandoned the under-center approach. 

26. Las Vegas Raiders (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Eventually this will be Fernando Mendoza’s team, but for now, Kirk Cousins appears to be up to the task. It will be interesting to see how this group looks against better competition, but from an offensive perspective, I’m not sure fans could have asked for anything more. 

27. New York Jets (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Not only did the offense perform better than expected, but the defense dominated what was expected to be an upbeat Titans offense, giving up less than 200 total yards and just 13 points. How sustainable will that be against better teams? We’ll find out next weekend when they host a Packers team desperate for a win.

28. Arizona Cardinals (1-0)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Similar to the Raiders, could Cardinals fans have asked for anything more in Week 1? Not only did they win, but of all the underdogs heading into Week 1, they had the most impressive win, taking down the Chargers. There’s still plenty of work to be done in Arizona, but this was a great start for the new regime. 

29. Atlanta Falcons (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Despite Tua’s back spasms that kept him out of Sunday’s game, the Falcons found a way to stick around on the road against a Steelers team that was in the playoffs a year ago. Although the immediate future doesn’t feel overly promising, the new regime in Atlanta should feel good about how they opened up the season on their third quarterback and against a tough opponent like Pittsburgh.

30. Tennessee Titans (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Although the thought process during a head coaching search is always to hire the best overall candidate, it’s worth wondering if the Titans did everything they could to set up Cam Ward for success. The offensive struggles have been well-documented in both training camp and now in Week 1. The only place to go is up from here, but Week 1 could not have gone much worse for the offense. 

31. Miami Dolphins (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: The former Packers contingent took over this Dolphins team knowing it would be an extensive rebuild, but after a convincing loss to the Raiders, it’s worth wondering just how far away this Dolphins team is from competing. Objective No. 1 is figuring out if Malik Willis can be their long-term starter.

32. Cleveland Browns (0-1)

Initial Week 1 Thought: Surprise, surprise. Deshaun Watson’s season-opening performance was one to forget. While some might look at his final numbers and assume he played OK, he was at his worst when the game got closer. There’s plenty of young talent on this roster, but until they have a viable option at quarterback, it’s hard to imagine this team being a fun watch for anyone.

item.title: Nick Sirianni explains why Eagles WR Hollywood Brown didn’t play Week 1
item.description: The Eagles head coach talked about Hollywood Brown, Dallas Goedert, the RB room, and much more.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles are 1-0 as the begin preparing for the Titans in Week 2, but head coach Nick Sirianni spoke with reporters on Monday after having a chance to watch Sunday’s film. He explained why Hollywood Brown didn’t play, and why they have to do better moving forward, as well as why Dallas Goedert is so clutch, and what he saw from the running backs against Washington.

When asked about certain individual performances, Sirianni kept coming back to this being the first game and everyone having things they need to improve. He spoke in support of Landon Dickerson following a rough performance, but shortly after the press conference, we learned the starting left guard was headed to IR.

Here’s what the head coach had to say:

On Hollywood Brown’s usage

Sirianni said that they were rotating guys on Sunday, and while they know Brown could help them, it just didn’t work out. The head coach emphasized that they want to get the WR the ball because his speed is real, but there are some games in which players get shut out of catches, and some games that they get shut out of reps.

“And quite frankly, just from my end, we want to get him in the football game. We’ll make a better effort to do that next time because I know the play making ability that he can bring with his speed but was pleased with how the wide outs played as a whole. Of course, there were things that you want back. They made a lot of plays down the field with different things with their job description. But I do want to see him in that football game and getting reps and contributing to this football team.”

On Dallas Goedert’s ability

Sirianni had a lot of positive things to say about Dallas Goedert, noting that the tight end has been so consistent throughout his time with the team.

“He just has a knack to make plays. He’s been very solid in the run game; thought he was solid yesterday in that as well. I think Dallas has had different versions of his game shine at different times. What I mean by that is yesterday you got to see him catch the ball over the middle in space and get to the right spot, be a big target, make plays and finish. You’ve also seen through Dallas’ career how much of a dangerous runner he is when the ball is in his hands and how hard he is to bring down. You got to see that a little bit yesterday on the third down.”

The head coach went on to talk about some of the more impressive moments from Goedert the past few years, highlighting some of his big sideline catches in critical playoff games. When the TE has to win one-on-one matchups, he’s able to do it in various ways on various routes, including some outside receiver routes and particularly in the red zone. Sirianni was sure to point out that Goedert’s success is not a surprise because he works his butt off to take his game to the next level.

“He’s a great teammate. He’s consistent. Guys love being around him, so it was good to see him have a good game yesterday. I was pumped for him, and obviously all the things he did to help our football team win last night.”

On the RB group

Sirianni disregarded the notion that Saquon Barkley’s 42-yard run was just an outlier compared to the rest of the performance, and insisted that the explosive play count just as much as the other ones.

“Being committed to the run game, sometimes that’s the way it goes. Not every play can be an explosive play in the run game. You want to make sure you’re staying ahead of the sticks. Now, that doesn’t mean that we ignore the issues that happened on those plays that averaged whatever. Some of them were negative plays, some of them were one-yard gains, some of them were six-yard gains. We’ll take those six-yard gains, but those plays count. When you’re committed to the run game like we are, you reap the benefits of that when you stick with it.”

The head coach also talked about Will Shipley being on the field in some critical moments. He explained that sometimes in third-down they don’t want to sub out a guy if they’re trying to go tempo.

“I think the best way to say, ‘Hey, why did Will Shipley get carries in those situations?’ Because we trust our backs. We trust every one of those guys. They’ve all shown to be able to make plays in different aspects. Obviously, Saquon’s our lead guy, as you guys know, and we’re really comfortable when Tank [Bigsby] and Will are in there and they’re getting carries and they’re getting protections. We’ve got a lot of faith in that group, and we’ll continue to have faith in that group because they continue to show us the things that they can do on a consistent basis.”

On Jalen Hurts’ development

“He made plays that only Jalen Hurts is capable of making at times across the entire league. With some of those new things that we were doing, I thought he did a nice job. Now, not a surprise to me. I was talking to somebody – we had 46 days or 47 days in training camp to get ready for that first game. We’re seeing that on a daily basis, that improvement.”

He also admitted that they wouldn’t have put in some of the different things they did on Sunday if they didn’t think Hurts could execute at a very high level.

On Makai Lemon’s debut

“[Makai Lemon has] always done a good job since he’s been here of blocking, doing the right things, being in the right spots. Obviously, the ones that went to him yesterday didn’t equal out to be big yardage gains, but he did little things to help us win the football game that sometimes are unseen and unnoticed. Why that’s really important is while a young player is continuing to get used to the NFL and being able to make an impact, you have to trust that player.

We trust him because he’s constantly doing the things without the ball that we need to help us win and that we know is going to help us win. That just builds confidence and allows players to develop, because I’ve been on the other side of that where maybe you didn’t trust the guy and you didn’t want to put him in there and then it was hard to get that guy going. So because of that trust we have in him, I think that’s going to help him continue to develop as a football player as we continue on through the season.”

item.title: Sunday Ticket prices increase, while NFL decreases the number of Sunday afternoon games
item.description: A quarter-century ago, NFL Sunday Ticket felt like a modern miracle to football fans.
item.content:encoded:
A quarter-century ago, NFL Sunday Ticket felt like a modern miracle to football fans. What once was an impossible dream, being able to watch any NFL game you wanted on Sunday afternoon, was now a reality. Fans who could previously only watch a game or two on Sunday could now have their pick of more than a dozen. It was an astonishing luxury to have all those games just a remote click away.

Sunday Ticket is still a popular item for football fans, but it has lost some luster. There are now so many opportunities to watch the NFL, on so many days of the week, that it's much easier for fans to feel like they're getting their fill by watching only the games that air on prime time or on their local affiliates on Sunday afternoon, without needing Sunday Ticket.

In 2002, the first season when the NFL had 32 teams, there were 17 Monday night games, 16 Sunday night games, three Thursday games and five Saturday games. Everything else was on Sunday afternoon.

In 2025, there were 21 Monday night games, 18 Sunday night games, six Sunday morning international games, 21 Thursday games (including three on Christmas Day), six Saturday games and two Friday games. Far fewer games were on Sunday afternoon.

So for the 2002 season, 215 of the NFL's 256 games (84 percent) were on Sunday afternoon. By 2025, when the season was one week longer, only 198 of 272 games (73 percent) were on Sunday afternoon.

Many Sunday Ticket subscribers get the service because they want to watch their favorite team, but don't live in their favorite team's market. But Sunday Ticket is increasingly unnecessary for fans of popular teams that are frequently shown on national television. Last year the Chiefs and Cowboys each played eight games that were either on Sunday night or another day of the week, and many of their Sunday afternoon games were shown across most of the country by Fox or CBS. If you're a Chiefs fan outside Kansas City or a Cowboys fan outside Dallas, it's a rare week when you need Sunday Ticket to watch your team.

And missing a game just isn't as big a deal today as it was in the early days of Sunday Ticket because there are so many opportunities to see what you're missing: If you have RedZone channel, you'll see all the big plays from every game, and even if you don't have RedZone, highlights are all over social media.

As the necessity of Sunday Ticket decreases, its prices increase: In 2023, YouTube took Sunday Ticket over from DirecTV, which had it from its inception. According to the Wall Street Journal, YouTube has increased the price of Sunday Ticket by almost 30 percent while the number of games available has declined.

The biggest NFL fans, the ones who love nothing more than spending a Sunday afternoon watching multiple games on multiple screens, will keep paying. But for a lot of fans, more money for fewer games is increasingly looking like a bad deal.

item.title: Bills news: Buffalo’s coaches react to season-opening win
item.description: While the Bills won in Houston, Joe Brady was concerned about penalties and said “all three phases weren’t good enough.”
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills won their season opener for the seventh time in their last 10 seasons, 36-31 over the Houston Texans. And they did it in a place that had previously served as a house of horrors: Houston, where Buffalo had lost its last four meetings and had not won since the 2006 season.

While the Bills are on a short week as they prepare to open their new Highmark Stadium Thursday night against the Detroit Lions, today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by hearing from head coach Joe Brady, offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, who offer up their key takeaways from Buffalo’s impressive season-opening win.

Check out the assessments below and then let us know your thoughts in the comments section.

What stood out and what needs to be improved after 36-31 win in Houston?

Head coach Joe Brady picked up the first win of his young coaching career Sunday vs. the Texans, but when he took the podium to address the media Monday, Brady said his team is still trying to learn more about itself and its playing style.

We “have a pulse, but you’re still trying to get a feel of how to use guys offensively, defensively, special teams, and to see the guys be able to make the adjustments; to see the guys be able to look through it all, be able to kind of play all the way through inside the red zone and figuring out, that’s what I was proud of,” Brady said.

Brady reflected on the impact DJ Moore had on the passing game in his Bills debut, Dalton Kincaid’s huge performance, the emotional return to Houston for defensive tackle Ed Oliver and why Oliver deserved a game ball; and how well his offensive line performed against a dominant Houston pass rush.

We also hear why defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard plans on limiting the number of snaps his defensive starters log and how his pass rushers, led by Greg Rousseau, enjoyed a dominant performance in Week 1. We then hear from offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael on the blossoming connection between Kincaid and Josh Allen and how the team successfully used 13 (one running back, three tight ends) personnel to stymie the Texans.

item.title: 53 Random Thoughts From Penn State’s 27-9 Victory Over Temple
item.description: You know the drill here. Random thoughts during my Penn State/Temple rewatch. 1. What a start to the game. Koby Howard just DUSTING the Temple secondary for a shot play to open us up. Surely, this was going to be a sign of things to come for the offense… 2. Well, maybe not. 3. I […]
item.content:encoded:
You know the drill here. Random thoughts during my Penn State/Temple rewatch.

1. What a start to the game. Koby Howard just DUSTING the Temple secondary for a shot play to open us up. Surely, this was going to be a sign of things to come for the offense…

2. Well, maybe not.

3. I talked about Rocco Becht yesterday in the Stock Up, Stock Down report, so I’m not going to use many (if any) random thoughts on him, but I’ll reiterate: really like what we’ve seen from him. I don’t know if he’s dramatically different from the Clifford/Allar half-decade we just went through, but he’s a fun watch and he at least has the aura of someone who knows what they are doing. He wasn’t perfect, but he was a big reason the offense at least got into second gear after the slow start.

4. On the 3rd & goal, give credit for Temple for bringing six when Penn State was going five out. No extra blocker back there and Rocco had essentially no time to even let the play develop. He has an extra half-second or so, he can try Koby on a fade or Brahmer coming across the middle.

5. I said this in the moment and it remains true: I was glad Ryan Barker missed that chip shot. He has been way too consistent and has made too many field goals. We need him to miss a couple here and there in inconsequential moments. Good miss. We continue to bark for Barker.

6. What are our takes on the Temple uniforms? I like them. Nice shade of red. The diamond usage is pretty unique to them, from what I can recall.

7. Zay Robinson is a fun player, man. Has shown nice chops back there returning kicks and punts, and in six offensive snaps on Saturday, he had 3 receptions for 34 yards. He’s someone whose stock is going up and I think we’ll see more and more as the season goes along.

8. This offense is funny because I think we all — the staff included, to be honest — had some questions about what the wide receivers were going to be. And through two games, they’ve answered those questions with really strong play basically across the unit of Koby, Chase Sowell, Brett Eskildsen, and Zay. I think they can go three or even four wide receiver much more often than maybe they originally thought.

9. Sorry to the 13 and 14 personnel. I still really like these tight ends, but as Gabe Burkle works his way back from injury, I think I’d go heavier on the two or even one tight end sets. These wide receivers are good! Let them cook!

10. I’d also be curious how that impacts the run game. When you have three or four tight ends on the field and you have them lined up tight, that’s bringing the defense in tight too and is taking away some space from the running backs. I’m not expecting the veer and shoot offense with the wide receivers lined up all the way out wide, but I do wonder if the running backs can find more success if you are — in theory — taking some defenders away from the box.

11. By the way, the running game: I don’t think it’s really on the offensive line. As Penn State fans, we’ve watched some *bad* offensive lines and this doesn’t seem like one of them.

12. Malachi Goodman might be a capital “D” Dude, by the way. He doesn’t look like a normal second-year player.

13. Josiah Zayas looked more like a freshman on Saturday, but look at where he lined up at one point in the first quarter.

14. That’s a true freshman corner/nickel/safety lining up as a standup defensive end. Shows you what this staff thinks of him to get him on the field this early and to line him up all over the place.

15. Pretty heavy snap logs for Keanu Williams (38) and Siale Taupaki (37) on a warm summer day in Philadelphia. That’s around 66% of the snaps, which is a bit on the higher side for a defensive tackle — especially ones in the 320-pound area.

16. Penn State was without Armstrong Nnodim and Alijah Carnell again, but it *feels* like those guys should be back for Big Ten play. Ideally though, would like to work them into the Buffalo game.

17. Pass rush wasn’t fantastic on Saturday, and the season-ending injury of Max Granville certainly played a part in that. Feel for the kid, who had just worked his way back from last offseason’s season-ending injury. That’s two seasons in a row down the drain for an uber-talented kid. Sucks.

18. Without Granville, I think defensive end is still in an OK spot, but it basically means Caleb Bacon is there full-time now. I imagine the original plan for him was to mostly play defensive end but get some linebacker looks against teams like Wisconsin, Minnesota, etc., but I don’t think Penn State wants to go super deep into the defensive end depth. It’ll need to be Bacon, Ikenna Ezeogu, Yvan Kemajou, and Alex McPherson.

19. Pray for health for the rest of those guys.

20. On the good news side of the injury front, good to see Alex Tatsch back out there. Didn’t do a whole ton, but did get 24 snaps in.

21. Kooper Ebel wearing #8 and Cael Brezina wearing #9 is going to confuse me all year. Even with Ebel’s hair coming out of his helmet, I still get them confused.

22. Got an extended look at Brezina — 21 snaps. Game was moving a bit too quickly for him at times. Took some poor angles and missed a tackle or two.

23. Ditto for Marcus Neal. This will be a game he’ll want to forget.

24. Tony Rojas’ interception really displayed his football IQ. He’s brought on a blitz and realizes he’s not going to get home, so he drops back into coverage and boom, right there was the football.

25. Penn State not scoring there was bad. Thanks for coming to my TEDTalk!

26. Peoples cutting this outside instead of right up the middle…not ideal.

27. This wouldn’t have been a touchdown or anything, but this was for sure blocked to be a run on the inside. Instead, Peoples takes it outside and the blocking isn’t right — stopped for no gain.

28. Second and third down, they go with 14 personnel and there’s not much of anything. Carson Hansen actually did a nice job making something out of nothing on second down to get three yards but both run plays had no shot from the snap.

29. I realize I am the Fullback Guy, so I’d like to point out all these guys are 6-foot-3+, none of them have neck rolls, and they would never take a handoff. You can line a tight end up at fullback, but that does NOT make them a fullback.

30. Like I said about Barker, I’m OK with a whoopsies from Taylor Mouser here on the run-run-run on the first three downs. It’s Temple, try to establish #culture and the running game. I just think with tight ends like Benjamin Brahmer and Andrew Rappleyea, they can get really creative in the red zone.

31. Tough misfire from Becht on 4th & goal. He had Rappleyea crossing and put way too much pace on the ball and it was a bit behind him. Game probably *feels* a lot different if that’s completed for a touchdown.

32. The keeper from Jaxon Smolik was nice. Shades of Sean Clifford against Michigan in 2022. Jeremiah Cooper has to make that tackle though. Look at this screen grab here:

33. If Smolik is doing that to ya, Colton Joseph, Bryce Underwood, and Demond Williams are licking their chops.

34. You just know Andy Kotelnicki saw Smolik take off and said “SEE!” #Iowa2025SmolikPackage

35. Temple not getting a touchdown on that drive sealed their fate. A drive like that — 91 yards, 15 plays, over eight minutes — needs to end with 6, not 3, in an upset bid.

36. Alright, I spent way too many thoughts on just the first quarter. Going to move this thing a long.

37. Chase Sowell had a very nice day, but the drop in the second quarter on what would have been a 47-yard touchdown is one he’ll want to have back.

38. Penn State started 1-5 on third down; ended 5-7.

39. 32 seconds. Slant to Brahmer for 9 yards to the 23 yard line. Clock does not stop at 26 seconds. Penn State has two timeouts. They snap the ball with 13 seconds.

40. That *has* to be a timeout there. If it was a goal-to-go situation, OK, you only have 3 more plays anyway. But they wasted anyway half the clock and were fortunate that the very next play was a touchdown.

41. That touchdown felt good though and was needed from a vibes perspective.

42. We’re only two games in, but I’ll be honest, Chase Sowell is better than I thought he’d be. I thought he’d be Saeed Blacknell-ish, but he’s much smoother than I anticipated. Intriguing kid at 6-foot-3, 203 pounds.

43. This fireball to Zay Robinson was sick.

44. Goes without saying, but a very good game from Brahmer. Quiet against Marshall for sure, but you saw Rocco go to Brahmer in some key spots on Saturday. The rapport they have is nice, and Brahmer can do some things with the ball in his hand. Fluid 6-foot-7 kid.

45. #18 is a great tight end number, too. Shades of Jesse James.

46. Count me in on the Koby Howard at running back package. Would like to see Zay Robinson there as well.

47. 3rd & 8 with under a minute to go in the third, ball on the 24, and Taylor Mouser fires up a run play that goes for 3 yards. Not really sure I’m following the logic on that one with the way Rocco was playing.

48. I’m good with Penn State not going for it on 4th down there. Field goal makes it a 20-3 game as you head into the fourth quarter, and it was clear Temple didn’t have three scores in them. Put the game on ice right there. I just don’t get the conservative run call given the game situation.

49. Loved the team coming to Rocco’s defense after the late hit by FORMER PENN STATE PLAYER Kolin Dinkins.

50. #66, redshirt freshman Will Tompkins, was the first one ready to go. Donnoe Harbour and Vaea Ikakoula were right behind. Cooper Cousins and Anthony Donkoh, former teammates with Dinkins, came in as well. Rocco was talking that good-good when he got up as well.

51. Just things you love to see, folks. The late hit being from a player who was on last year’s Penn State team feels symbolic too, doesn’t it?

52. Passable, middling game from Penn State, all things considered. The team — and the fan base — probably needed the B-/C+ performance after the A+ performance against Marshall. A performance to ground ourselves and remember: this is a long season. Not every game will be perfect, but game 2 of many more to come.

53. Shoutout the Philly-area Penn State faithful. We are Philadelphia’s college football team.

item.title: The Panthers could add some backend versatility early in the NFL Draft
item.description: Let’s take a closer look at one of the prospects the Panthers could select in the 2026 NFL Draft.
item.content:encoded:
The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Georgia Bulldogs safety KJ Bolden.

Bio

Bolden (6’0”, 185 lbs.) was a consensus five-star recruit out of Buford, GA and the top ranked safety coming out of high school. He played both sides of the ball for his high school football team and was an anchor on the track team. Bolden had originally committed to Florida State, but he decided to switch to his hometown Bulldogs late in the process. True freshman don’t normally see the field much at programs like Georgia, but Bolden was an exception. He played in all 14 games his true freshman season, even finishing fifth on the team in tackles. He added a sack, a forced fumble, and an interception, helping him earn an SEC All-Freshman nod. After starter Malachi Starks left for the NFL last year, Bolden stepped up in his place. He finished second on the team in tackles as the full time starter with 76 stops, also tallying two interceptions, five passes defended, a fumble recovery, and a blocked punt. His performance earned him Second Team All-SEC honors and a spot on many of the defender award watch lists for this season. A couple games into this season, Bolden has three tackles and 1.5 for loss in two blowout wins against cupcake opponents where he was taken out early in the game to let the backups get some experience.

Strengths/Weaknesses

Bolden’s athleticism jumps off the tape as he boasts legitimate 4.33 speed. He uses that athleticism to full effect both in the box and in single-high situations, breaking on passes and filling in run gaps as good or better than any other safety in college football. He is a competent and willing tackler, only tagged with four missed tackles last season on about 80 chances. Bolden does an excellent job of keeping his eyes on the quarterback, reading and planting to jump routes and contest catches. He also has positional versatility as a box safety, a deep safety, and even a slot defender.

Bolden’s slight frame at just 185 lbs. is the most concerning flaw in his game. Bigger bodied backs and receivers can really test his strength because of his lass of mass. Along those lines, he struggles at times against NFL caliber tight ends in man coverage. Those guys are typically larger and heavier, bullying him a bit in coverage. Many scouts would also like to see more takeaways this year from Bolden: he has the range and ability to take the football away, just needs to do it more consistently.

Projection

Bolden’s combination of speed, tackling, and versatility make him a likely first round selection. He should be able to put some mass on his frame at the next level, so even if he doesn’t ever become an Ed Reed type of playmaker on the backend he’ll have a spot in the NFL. After the Panthers defense allowed 59 points and over 250 rushing yards against the Bears, having a sure tackling center fielder would help out a lot. Regardless of whether Ejiro Evero’s scheme is still in Carolina next year or not, Bolden’s versatility allows him to still be on the Panthers radar come April.

What do you think, Panthers fans? If KJ Bolden is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

item.title: 5 things we learned from the Steelers’ Week 1 snap counts
item.description: Payton Wilson played more, T.J. Watt played less in the win over the Falcons.
item.content:encoded:
Snap counts are just one statistic, but they do provide some clarity on the real hierarchy of a team’s depth chart when coaches tend to play coy in press conferences.

After just one game, the Steelers’ depth is sure to change over the upcoming weeks of the season — and when facing teams that aren’t the Cooper Rush-led Falcons.

Still, there are some lessons we can learn from Pittsburgh’s snap counts Week 1.

T.J. Watt, Cam Heyward getting more rest

This was one of the biggest takeaways from defensive coordinator Patrick Graham’s new Steelers scheme: workhorse veteran defenders T.J. Watt and Cam Heyward actually had time to catch their breath in-game versus the Falcons.

Watt actually played the least amount of defensive snaps of the Steelers’ big three at outside linebacker with 38, but he was in the same range as Nick Herbig (39) and Alex Highsmith (41). Jack Sawyer contributed another 23.

The increased rotation seemed to work, with Watt and Highsmith each recording two-sack games. Herbig (who played some off-ball linebacker versus Atlanta) and Sawyer weren’t left off the stat sheet either, combining for six total tackles.

Heyward had an even larger reduction in snaps. After being the top-snapped defensive lineman in the entire NFL last season at age 36, the now-37-year-old played just 32 snaps (53%) defensively. Across the rest of the defensive line, Keeanu Benton logged 35 snaps, Derrick Harmon 24, and Yahya Black and Sebastian Joseph-Day had 18 each.

Like Watt, Heyward responded with a monster game, still making an impact as a rusher and run defender, but recording an impressive three batted passes.

Jalen Ramsey, Payton Wilson are every-down players

Veteran defensive back Jalen Ramsey is set to count $17.2 million against the cap this year — it’s no surprise the Steelers want him to earn that on the field. It wasn’t exactly a surprise, but the Steelers took advantage of Ramsey’s versatility quite a bit against the Falcons, lining him up in the slot when in nickel defense, and moving him to safety opposite Jaquan Brisker in base.

The end result was Ramsey playing all 61 of the Steelers’ defensive snaps on Sunday, with free agent addition Rayshawn Jenkins only recording 32 at safety.

It’ll be interesting to see what the Steelers do with Ramsey after starting safety DeShon Elliott returns from injured reserve. Will the Steelers still pull a starting safety off the field for Ramsey in formations without a slot defender? Or will Ramsey start seeing more rest alongside Watt and Heyward?

Slightly more notable was inside linebacker Payton Wilson playing 58 of the team’s 61 defensive snaps. Wilson struggled late in 2025, losing snaps to Malik Harrison, but seems to have returned to the role of an every-down linebacker.

That trust from Graham was rewarded against Atlanta, where Wilson was all over the field, recording a team-best 13 total tackles.

Germie Bernard still has work to do

One player who was barely featured on Sunday was rookie second-round wide receiver Germie Bernard, who logged just three of the team’s 67 total offensive snaps.

Roman Wilson, on the other hand, showed a clear lead in the team’s WR3 role with 37 snaps.

After spending such high draft capital on Bernard, the Steelers still clearly have big plans for the rookie down the road. But for now, it looks like the WR3 job is Wilson’s to lose.

Darnell Washington still a big part of the offense

After being an extremely tight end-heavy team in 2025 under offensive coordinator Arthur Smith, the Steelers have shifted in a more 11 personnel-friendly direction under head coach Mike McCarthy.

Still, the Steelers have two of the NFL’s top-15 highest-paid tight ends, and the team made sure to use both against the Falcons, playing Pat Freiermuth for 49 snaps and Darnell Washington for 43.

Freiemuth had a bit of a bounce-back performance after a quiet 2025, recording five catches for 46 yards and a score against Atlanta. Washington had just two grabs for 18 yards, but managed a highlight-worthy stiff arm and remained a key run blocker for the team.

One of the biggest departures from the Arthur Smith era, beyond Freiermuth once again looking like a TE1, was a lack of heavy TE3 usage. Robert Tonyan logged just two offensive snaps Sunday, although Riley Nowakowski did see eight in a fullback/H-back role.

Core special teamers emerge

As expected, the Steelers have a new group of primary special teamers this season. However, standouts such as Carson Bruener (24 snaps — 80%), Ben Skowronek (18) and Jack Sawyer (24) remained big pieces of the third phase of the game.

Rookies Robert Spears-Jennings (23 snaps), Daylen Everette (16), Riley Nowakowski (17), Eli Heidenreich (13) and returner Kaden Wetjen (10) were also contributors.

Interestingly, Nick Herbig isn’t off special teams duties yet despite signing a big contract this offseason. He logged 11 special teams snaps on Sunday, while T.J. Watt and Alex Highsmith each had zero.

While some veteran backups such as Rayshawn Jenkins (10 snaps), Cole Holcomb (17) and Brandin Echols (20) were big parts of Pittsburgh’s special teams, Tonyan (three) did not see many snaps in that phase of the game.

item.title: Bengals Tuesday Trenches: 1-0 and ready for Houston
item.description: After sinking some pirates, the Bengals are off to Houston to face…. people from Texas?
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals are 1-0 after defeating the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at home by a score of 33-27 on Sunday. For the first time in Joe Burrow’s career, he’s won Week 1 games in back-to-back seasons, and while it wasn’t always pretty, the Bengals soundly defeated a pretty solid team that should push for the NFC South title.

There’s a lot to talk about, so here are some things that stood out to me:

  • First, I was a little shocked that Landon Robinson was a healthy scratch. I get that he’s a seventh-round pick, but I thought he played really well throughout the preseason. Having too many defensive tackles is a good problem to have, I guess, but I was hoping to see the young kid—especially after seeing him arrive for his first NFL game in his dress uniform from the Naval Academy.
  • I’m convinced at this point that Burrow is just a slow starter. He wasn’t terrible on Sunday, but he wasn’t his normal self, and his pick-six thrown to linebacker Josiah Trotter was very un-Burrow-like. I’m not overly concerned about the offense, though. There’s way too much talent for this group not to find its stride.
  • It’s clear the Bengals really do want to emphasize Burrow playing under center to set up the play-action game. I can see the potential, even if Burrow doesn’t look completely comfortable with it yet.
  • Amarius Mims absolutely shut down the Bucs’ first-round pick Rueben Bain Jr. Had the Bengals not traded the No. 10 overall selection for Dexter Lawrence, I would have liked to see them land Bain. Instead, Mims—whose arms are six inches longer than Bain’s—just kept him completely out of the game. It’s not that Bain won’t be good (though his short arms might be an issue), but I think Mims has the potential to become one of the best right tackles in the league.
  • Boye Mafe was outstanding. He had a sack, a tackle for loss, multiple hurries, a forced fumble and a fumble recovery. I still think Trey Hendrickson is probably the best free-agent signing the Bengals have pulled off over the last decade or so, but Mafe showed Sunday that he could potentially fill those big shoes.
  • Al Golden’s defense had waves of pressure coming from all directions. Baker Mayfield was sacked four times, with five different players getting credit for them. The Bucs aren’t a bad team, and bringing down Mayfield four times while forcing four turnovers was huge.
  • With the Bengals’ slow offensive start, I doubt they win this game without the additions of Lawrence, Mafe, Jonathan Allen and Bryan Cook.
  • Tackling was still an issue on Sunday, but I’m willing—for now—to write it off as Week 1 jitters. Players were generally in the right place at the right time, but there were several instances where Bucs players bounced off tackles and picked up extra yards. That needs to be cleaned up.
  • I questioned the Bengals’ decision to stick with Demetrius Knight Jr. and Barrett Carter in 2026. They missed six tackles between them—three each—sharing the team leads in that category. However, they both made some great plays, including Knight’s touchdown and Carter’s sack and forced fumble. With the deep and talented defensive line in front of them, I think I could get on board with the duo… as long as they stop missing tackles.
  • Samaje Perine is still a pretty big part of the Bengals’ offense. Tahj Brooks only took two offensive snaps all day.
  • Burrow was sacked only once, and that sack was given up by tight end Drew Sample. The offensive line played very well all day long.
  • The defensive line was outstanding, too.
  • When was the last time we could say that about both the Bengals’ offensive and defensive lines?
  • Lawrence had PFF’s highest pass-rushing grade on the Bengals’ defense (71.1) and was credited with one hit and two hurries. He had an 18.2% pass-rush win rate, which was best on the team and seventh-best in the league before Monday Night Football.
  • Worth every little bit of that No. 10 overall selection.
  • If you’re worried about Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, don’t be. They’re going to be just fine. Instead, be thankful the Bengals held on to Mike Gesicki, who essentially served as WR3 and found himself in space all day long. Let teams focus all their attention on the best wide-receiver duo in the league. Burrow will find someone else.

There’s more, but we need to talk a little about the Houston Texans.

The Bengals head to Houston to face the Texans, who have, in my opinion, the worst team name in the NFL.

You’re named the Texans because you’re proud to be from Texas? Neat.

The Bengals were named after a professional football team that existed in Cincinnati in the late ’30s and early ’40s. Plus, in a battle between your average Bengal tiger and your average dude from Texas (no weapons)… well, I’ll always put my money on the giant murder cat.

Now that I’ve gotten that off my chest, I do think the Texans are a good team.

They lost at home in Week 1 to a very good Buffalo Bills team by a score of 36-31, but they nearly pulled off the upset. Houston took a one-point lead in the fourth quarter but couldn’t keep Josh Allen and company out of the end zone.

The Texans don’t want to start the season 0-2 and losing both games in front of their home crowd, and they’re going to come out swinging to make sure that doesn’t happen.

The Bengals can win this game. I think they’re the better team, but they’ll need to clean up some of the issues from Week 1 if they want to head to Pittsburgh in Week 3 with a 2-0 record.

Quick thoughts from around the AFC North:

  • The Steelers beat Cooper Rush and the Falcons in Pittsburgh by a score of 20-13. Color me unimpressed.
  • The Ravens went to Indy and beat the pants off the Colts, 41-23. Derrick Henry, who is somehow still doing this at 32 years old, carried the ball 24 times for 144 yards and three touchdowns. Color me impressed.
  • The Browns are the Browns.

The score was closer than the game ever really felt on Sunday, but that doesn’t mean there aren’t things the Bengals need to clean up. They got the most important thing they needed from Week 1—a win.

Now comes Houston.

And if they don’t clean up a handful of those mistakes, they won’t be leaving Texas with another one.

All my exes live in Texas
And Texas is the place I’d dearly love to be
But all my exes live in Texas
Therefore I reside in Tennessee

item.title: Biggest surprises from the Detroit Lions’ Week 1 win over Saints
item.description: Highlighting the biggest surprises from the Detroit Lions’ Week 1 win over the New Orleans Saints.
item.content:encoded:
Week 1 in the NFL is thrilling for so many reasons. For one, it’s just the return of football, the passion of millions of people around the world.

But for a league with the longest offseason, it’s also the culmination of months and months of work from each team’s front office. Every free agent signing, waiver wire claim, draft pick, undrafted free agent signing—it all comes together to paint a picture when the teams finally take the field. I’ve likened it before to Christmas morning. After seeing these gifts under the tree for months, we finally get to unwrap it and see what we’ve got.

Since early January, we’ve all outlined how we would’ve approached the offseason, criticized and/or praised every move Detroit Lions general manager Brad Holmes opted to make, and it was all just educated guessing. On Sunday night, we finally had a data point that matters. Was Holmes’ plan the best to set the Lions up for current and future success? We got a taste in their 31-30 victory of the New Orleans Saints.

Some things went as expected, others most certainly did not. So today’s Question of the Day is:

What was the biggest surprise from the Lions’ Week 1 win over the Saints?

My answer: I’m going to stick with the positive here, because—quite frankly—most of the negative things from Sunday’s game were somewhat expected. The secondary struggled, the defense gave up more explosive plays, and the offense looked like a product that was still putting pieces together. Perhaps the biggest negative shock was the rough day from Jameson Williams, particularly after a strong training camp.

But the biggest surprise to me was just how effective the Lions’ running game was. I thought it was fully reasonable and expected for the offensive line to take some time to come together. With Cade Mays’ injury, a left guard battle that never really got off the ground, and a rookie right tackle, everything was set up for some early chemistry issues. And when Ben Bartch, who barely got any first-team work in training camp, had to step in for an injured Christian Mahogany in the first quarter, I only expected more trouble.

Instead, we saw the Lions post a rushing success rate better than they averaged during Ben Johnson’s best years in Detroit:

Through Week 1, the Lions rank eighth in PFF’s team run blocking grade (69.7), fifth in adjusted line yards (5.16), and third in yards before contact (73). Those are all serious indicator that the Lions were moving people in the run game.

I credit the players themselves for creating a cohesive unit through some early adversity. Certainly offensive line coach Hank Fraley deserves some credit. And new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, who has been widely praised specifically for his scheme in the run game, clearly put his players in the best position to succeed.

While the overall offensive performance was inconsistent, and there are legitimate questions to have about Petzing’s play calling, I was extremely encouraged and somewhat surprised that Detroit’s running game appears to be back—especially against a Saints team that ranked eighth in run defense DVOA, second in run defense EPA, and ninth in success rate allowed last season.
